text: Aachen, 796 CE: Charlemagne builds his palace chapel.
evidence: Charlemagne started the chapel around 796, alongside the rest of the palace complex (search summary, not a verbatim quote).

text: Aachen, 936 CE: First of 31 royal coronations here.
evidence: The original Palatine Chapel hosted the coronation of thirty-one German kings from 936 to 1531 (search summary, not a verbatim quote). Other sources give 30 or more.

text: Agra, 1556 CE: Akbar's capital.
evidence: Akbar (r. 1556–1605) made Agra his capital, then shifted temporarily to Fatehpur Sikri between 1571 and 1585 (search summary, not a verbatim quote).

text: Agra, 1648 CE: Mughal capital moves to Delhi.
evidence: Delhi became the capital in 1648 during the rule of Shah Jahan (search summary, not a verbatim quote). Some other sources say 1649 or 1658.
fix: Optionally note that the move was gradual and that some sources date it to 1649 or 1658.

text: Agra, 1653 CE: Taj Mahal completed.
evidence: The complex is believed to have been completed in its entirety in 1653 (search summary, not a verbatim quote).

text: Akhetaten (Amarna), 1887 CE: Amarna letters found.
evidence: They were first discovered around 1887 by local Egyptians who secretly dug most of them from the ruined city of Amarna (search summary, not a verbatim quote).

text: Akhetaten (Amarna), 1332 BCE: Abandoned under Tutankhamun.
evidence: Perhaps after only two years he had left Akhetaten to reign from Memphis (search summary, not a verbatim quote). Akhenaten died in 1332 BC and the city was abandoned shortly afterwards.
fix: The exact year is uncertain. Say c. 1330 BCE, or 'soon after Akhenaten's death in 1332 BCE'.

text: Akhetaten (Amarna), 1346 BCE: Akhenaten founds it.
evidence: The city was established in 1346 BC at the direction of the Pharaoh Akhenaten, and abandoned shortly after his death in 1332 BC (search summary, not a verbatim quote). Another source gives about 1349 BC.

text: Aksum, 330 CE: King Ezana adopts Christianity.
fix: Optionally say 'around 330 (traditional date)'. Sources give about 324 to 333, and one scholarly argument puts it in the 340s.

sources.cite: Christianity and the Queen of Sheba (SFU Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology) (sfu.ca)

text: Aksum, 960 CE: Sacked by Queen Gudit (by tradition).
evidence: around 960 a Jewish queen named Gudit defeated the empire and burned its churches and literature

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Ethiopia in the Middle Ages

text: Aleppo, 1138 CE: Great earthquake.
evidence: The 1138 Aleppo earthquake struck northern Syria on 11 October 1138.

text: Aleppo, 1260 CE: Sacked by Hulagu's Mongols.
evidence: The siege lasted from 17 January to 24 January 1260.

text: Aleppo, 1400 CE: Sacked by Timur.
evidence: Sack dated October–November 1400.

text: Aleppo, 1822 CE: Earthquake kills thousands.
evidence: Casualties are listed as 20,000–60,000, with 20,000 regarded as the more likely number.

text: Aleppo, 2016 CE: Four-year battle ends.
evidence: The battle is dated from 19 July 2012 to 22 December 2016.

text: Aleppo, 637 CE: Taken by Arab armies.
evidence: The siege is dated August–October 637, with Khalid ibn al-Walid and Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah commanding.
fix: Optional: another Wikipedia article (Iyad ibn Ghanm) places Iyad's capture of Aleppo in 638.

text: Aleppo, 1800 BCE: Capital of the kingdom of Yamhad.
evidence: Wikipedia's dating is c. 1800–1525 BC, while its Yamhad infobox gives c. 1810 BC–c. 1517 BC.

text: Alexandria, 1798 CE: Napoleon lands; a town of ~8,000.
evidence: 1800 listed as the city's low point, population 8,000; French forces under Napoleon Bonaparte besiege and conquer what is now just a town.
fix: The 8,000 figure is Wikipedia's estimate for 1800. Universalis gives 5,000–7,000 for 1798. Write 'a town of ~5,000–8,000'.

text: Alexandria, 1882 CE: Bombarded by the British.
evidence: The British Mediterranean Fleet bombarded Alexandria, Egypt, on 11–13 July 1882, during the Anglo-Egyptian War.

text: Alexandria, 365 CE: Tsunami from the Crete earthquake.
evidence: The earthquake struck on the morning of 21 July 365 and produced a tsunami that devastated the southern and eastern coasts of the Mediterranean, particularly Libya, Alexandria, and the Nile Delta.

text: Alexandria, 641 CE: Taken by Arab armies.
evidence: The siege ran from March to September 641, and the Rashidun Caliphate took the Byzantine port.
fix: Optional: the treaty was signed in November 641 and the city was handed over in September 642.

text: Alexandria, 331 BCE: Founded by Alexander.
evidence: Alexandria was founded by Alexander the Great in 331 BC (the exact date is disputed).

text: Alexandria, 48 BCE: Caesar's fire.
evidence: Caesar tells us in his Civil Wars that he burned all the ships in the docks and that the fire spread, destroying many of the surrounding buildings (3.111).
fix: Do not imply the library burned. The 48 BCE fire is attested, but the library's destruction is not.

sources.cite: Did Julius Caesar Burn Down the Library of Alexandria? (badancient.com)

text: Amsterdam, 1602 CE: Dutch East India Company founded.
evidence: The Dutch East India Company (VOC) was founded on 20 March 1602, when the States General of the Netherlands merged existing trading companies into one.

text: Amsterdam, 1609 CE: Exchange Bank founded.
evidence: The bank began operating on January 31, 1609 (search summary of the page).

text: Amsterdam, 1672 CE: French invasion: the 'disaster year'.
evidence: In 1672 the Dutch Republic was attacked by France, England, Münster and Cologne, the 'Disaster Year' (Rampjaar) (paraphrased from the search summary).

text: Angkor, 1150 CE: Angkor Wat completed.
evidence: Suryavarman II (r. 1113-1150 CE) ordered Angkor Wat in the early 12th century. One timeline source gives c. 1160 for completion, and the pages say the temple may never have been finished (paraphrased from the search summary).
fix: Say it was built under Suryavarman II (r. 1113–1150) in the early 12th century. Completion is uncertain: some sources say c. 1150, one says c. 1160, and it may have been left unfinished.

text: Angkor, 1177 CE: Sacked by the Cham.
evidence: In 1177 the Cham fleet came up the Mekong, across Tonlé Sap and the Siem Reap River. They pillaged the capital Yasodharapura and killed king Tribhuvanadityavarman (paraphrased from the search summary).

text: Angkor, 1181 CE: Jayavarman VII rebuilds as Angkor Thom.
evidence: Jayavarman VII was crowned in 1181 after expelling the Chams. He built the walled and moated city of Angkor Thom with the Bayon at its centre (paraphrased from the search summary).

text: Angkor, 1431 CE: Ayutthaya attacks.
evidence: The article dates Ayutthaya's capture of Angkor to 1431, after a siege of Angkor Thom that began in 1430 (paraphrased from the search summary). One other page, Borommarachathirat II, gives 1433.

text: Angkor, 802 CE: Jayavarman II proclaimed king.
evidence: Historians generally date the start of the Angkor period to 802, when Jayavarman II held a consecration ritual on Mahendraparvata (Phnom Kulen) (paraphrased from the search summary).

text: Antakya, 1098 CE: Taken by the First Crusade.
evidence: The crusaders took Antioch on 3 June 1098, after a siege that began in October 1097 (paraphrased from the search summary).

text: Antakya, 115 CE: Earthquake nearly kills Emperor Trajan.
evidence: Trajan was staying in Antioch while preparing a campaign against the Parthians... he barely escaped death by climbing out the window of the house where he was staying, sustaining only minor injuries.

text: Antakya, 1268 CE: Destroyed by Baybars.
evidence: on May 18, 1268, Baibars ordered a general assault. The walls were breached, and the inhabitants surrendered.
fix: Optional: say 'Captured and sacked by Baybars'. The sources describe the capture and massacre, not the physical destruction of the whole city.

text: Antakya, 2023 CE: Türkiye–Syria earthquake.
evidence: Antakya was among the hardest-hit cities in the February 6, 2023 earthquakes.

sources.cite: Turkey's Antakya is in ruins after the quake, erasing cultural and religious heritage (vermontpublic.org)

text: Antakya, 526 CE: Earthquake kills perhaps 250,000.
evidence: Estimates vary between 250,000 and 300,000, with 250,000 being the most commonly reported.

text: Antakya, 540 CE: Sacked by Persia's Khosrow I.
evidence: He sacked the major city of Antioch and deported its population to Persia.

text: Antwerp, 1576 CE: Spanish Fury sack.
evidence: Mutinying Spanish troops began the sack on 4 November 1576, and the violence lasted about three days.

text: Antwerp, 1585 CE: Falls to Spain; the Scheldt is closed.
evidence: Antwerp surrendered on 17 August 1585... Afterward, the Dutch fleet kept the Scheldt blocked, cutting the city off from sea trade.

text: Anuradhapura, 993 CE: Sacked by the Chola.
evidence: they sacked Anuradhapura in A.D. 993 and annexed Rajarata.

text: Anuradhapura, 250 BCE: Buddhism arrives with Ashoka's son Mahinda.
evidence: Introduction of Theravada Buddhism, dated to 250 BCE (paraphrase of the search summary; I did not see the page's exact wording). Mahinda, son of Ashoka, met King Devanampiya Tissa at Mihintale.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Timeline of Sri Lankan history

text: Yin (Anyang), 1899 CE: Oracle bones identified in Beijing medicine shops.
evidence: Wang Yirong, then chancellor of the Imperial Academy, fell ill with malaria in 1899 and was sent to an apothecary for "dragon bones" (paraphrase of the search summary).

text: Yin (Anyang), 1046 BCE: Zhou conquest.
evidence: The battle is dated to about 1046 BC; the Zhou defeated the Shang at Muye and captured the Shang capital Yin (paraphrase of the search summary).

text: Yin (Anyang), 1200 BCE: Oracle-bone inscriptions.
evidence: Inscriptions from Wu Ding's reign have been radiocarbon dated to 1254–1197 BC (paraphrase of the search summary).

text: Athens, 1458 CE: Ottoman conquest.
evidence: The Acropolis held out until June 1458, when it surrendered, and Mehmed II entered Athens in August 1458 (paraphrase of the search summary). Some sources say the city itself fell in 1456.
fix: 1458 is the year the Acropolis fell and Mehmed visited. If you mean the city's first surrender, some sources give 1456. Consider wording it as 'Ottomans take Athens (1456–58)'.

text: Athens, 1687 CE: Venetian shell blows up the Parthenon.
evidence: Venetian artillery under Francesco Morosini ignited the Ottoman gunpowder stored in the Parthenon on 26 September 1687 (paraphrase of the search summary).

sources.cite: On This Day in 1687: Venetians' Artillery Devastates the Parthenon (greekcitytimes.com)

text: Athens, 1834 CE: Capital of independent Greece.
evidence: Athens was made Greece's capital in 1834, on 18 September (paraphrase of the search summary).

sources.cite: On this day in 1834, Athens became the capital city of Greece (greekcitytimes.com)

text: Athens, 387 BCE: Plato founds the Academy.
evidence: Plato set up the Academy in Athens around 387 BC; some sources say 388 or 385 BC (paraphrase of the search summary).

text: Athens, 404 BCE: Loses the Peloponnesian War.
evidence: Athens surrendered in 404 BCE, about a year after its fleet was destroyed at Aegospotami.

text: Athens, 432 BCE: Parthenon completed.
evidence: Construction began in 447 BC and the building was substantially finished by 438 BC; work on the decorations continued until at least 433 (the pediment sculptures were probably in place by 432).
fix: Say the building was completed in 438 BCE. The sculptural decoration was finished around 432 BCE.

sources.cite: Parthenon (Wikipedia CD selection, hosted at EPFL) (dlab.epfl.ch)

text: Athens, 480 BCE: Burned by Xerxes' Persians.
evidence: The city fell in September 480 BCE during the second Persian invasion, and Xerxes ordered it torched.

text: Athens, 508 BCE: Cleisthenes' democratic reforms.
evidence: Cleisthenes issued reforms in 508 and 507 BC that undermined the domination of the aristocratic families.

text: Athens, 86 BCE: Sacked by Sulla.
evidence: Sulla's forces sacked Athens on the night of 1 March 86 BC after a siege of several months.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Siege of Athens and Piraeus (87–86 BC)

text: Ayutthaya, 1351 CE: Founded by King U Thong.
evidence: U Thong was the founder and first monarch of the Ayutthaya Kingdom, reigning from 1351 to 1369.

text: Ayutthaya, 1767 CE: Destroyed by Burmese armies.
evidence: On 7 April 1767, Burmese forces set fire to the base of the city wall at Hua Ro and bombarded the city. The city was destroyed and looted, and then set ablaze.

text: Babylon, 1595 BCE: Sacked by the Hittites.
evidence: Mursili's forces took Babylon around 1595 BC, after first conquering Aleppo (Yamhad).
fix: 1595 BCE follows the middle chronology. Other chronologies put the sack at 1587 BCE or 1531 BCE, so consider writing "c. 1595 BCE".

text: Babylon, 1792 BCE: Hammurabi's reign begins.
evidence: Wikipedia gives his reign as c. 1792 to c. 1750 BC, and notes that the 1792 date follows the middle chronology.
fix: Optionally say "c. 1792 BCE (middle chronology)", since other chronologies differ.

text: Babylon, 323 BCE: Alexander dies here.
evidence: A Babylonian astronomical diary places his death between the evening of 10 June and the evening of 11 June 323 BCE.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Death of Alexander the Great

text: Babylon, 539 BCE: Taken by Cyrus of Persia.
evidence: On October 12, 539 BC, the army of Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon.

text: Babylon, 575 BCE: Ishtar Gate built.
evidence: It was constructed in about 575 BC by order of King Nebuchadnezzar II on the north side of the city.

text: Babylon, 689 BCE: Destroyed by Sennacherib.
evidence: Babylon had been the target of most of his military campaigns and had caused the death of his son, so he destroyed the city in 689 BC.

text: Bagan, 1044 CE: Anawrahta founds the Pagan empire.
evidence: 1044 | 11 August | Anawrahta ascends to Pagan throne
fix: 1044 is the date Anawrahta took the throne. Sources date the founding of the Pagan Empire to the 1050s–1060s, after his conquests. Reword to "Anawrahta takes the throne and begins building the Pagan empire", or use the 1050s for the founding.

text: Bagan, 1287 CE: Mongol invasion.
evidence: The Battle of Pagan was fought in December 1287 between the Yuan dynasty and the Pagan Kingdom.
fix: Optional: the Mongol invasions began in 1277, and 1287 is the final campaign that ended the kingdom.

text: Baghdad, 1258 CE: Mongols sack the city and kill the caliph.
evidence: Hulegu had the caliph and one of his sons killed by the time-honoured method of being wrapped in felt and beaten to death as the army paused after leaving the city.

text: Baghdad, 1401 CE: Sacked by Timur.
evidence: Timur besieged the Jalayirid capital for forty days and then massacred residents who had resisted. The Turco-Mongol army looted the treasury and razed much of the city, except for mosques and madrasas.

text: Baghdad, 1534 CE: Ottoman conquest.
evidence: The first began with Sultan Süleyman I's conquest in 1534 and ended with the Safavid capture of Baghdad in 1623.

text: Baghdad, 1921 CE: Capital of the new Kingdom of Iraq.
evidence: Faisal was proclaimed as King of Iraq at Baghdad on 23rd August 1921, following a plebiscite amongst the Iraqi people.

text: Baghdad, 2003 CE: US-led invasion.
evidence: The invasion began on 20 March 2003 and lasted just over one month, including 26 days of major combat operations.

text: Baghdad, 762 CE: Founded by al-Mansur.
evidence: On 30 July 762 the caliph Al-Mansur commissioned the construction of the city.

text: Baghdad, 830 CE: House of Wisdom flourishes.
evidence: During the reign of al-Ma'mun, it was turned into a public academy and a library.
fix: Optional: say the House of Wisdom peaked under al-Ma'mun (r. 813–833). No source gives the year 830.

text: Bangkok, 1782 CE: Rama I makes it capital.
evidence: The City Pillar went up on 21 April 1782, which is regarded as the date of the foundation of Bangkok as the capital.

text: Beijing, 1215 CE: Sacked by Genghis Khan.
evidence: Mongol forces sacked the city after Genghis Khan left.
fix: Optional: name the city Zhongdu, the Jin capital on the site of present-day Beijing. It fell in May or June 1215.

text: Beijing, 1267 CE: Kublai Khan begins Dadu.
evidence: In 1267, Genghis Khan's grandson Kublai Khan designated it as his main capital, Dadu, and went on to found the Chinese-style Yuan dynasty there in 1271.
fix: The sources I found split the dates. Kublai designated Dadu as capital in 1267, ordered construction in 1266, and the city is given as founded in 1264. Reword to 'Kublai Khan orders Dadu built (1266) / makes it his capital (1267)'.

text: Beijing, 1420 CE: Forbidden City completed.
evidence: Work began in 1406 and the palace was finished in 1420 under the Yongle Emperor.

text: Beijing, 1900 CE: Boxer siege of the legations.
evidence: The siege ran from 20 June to 14 August 1900, and the defenders held out for 55 days until an international relief force broke through.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Siege of the International Legations

text: Beijing, 1949 CE: Mao proclaims the People's Republic.
evidence: Mao proclaimed the People's Republic from the Tiananmen Gate rostrum in Beijing on October 1, 1949.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Proclamation of the People's Republic of China

text: Benin City, 1897 CE: Sacked by a British expedition.
evidence: The 1897 Benin Expedition was a British military campaign that ended with the capture and destruction of Benin City; the city fell on February 18, 1897.

text: Berlin, 1871 CE: Capital of the German Empire.
evidence: Between 1871 and 1918, Berlin was the capital city of the German Empire.

sources.cite: How Berlin was the Capital of 5 Countries in Less than 100 Years (thecollector.com)

text: Berlin, 1945 CE: Falls to the Red Army.
evidence: The city's garrison surrendered on 2 May, but fighting continued around the city until 8 May.

text: Berlin, 1961 CE: Berlin Wall built.
evidence: Construction of the Berlin Wall was commenced by the government of the GDR on 13 August 1961.

text: Berlin, 1989 CE: The Wall falls.
evidence: The fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989 was triggered by a press conference error.

sources.cite: Fall of the Berlin Wall (Berlin, 9 November 1989) (cvce.eu)

text: Brugge, 1309 CE: Its 'Beurs' gives the word bourse.
evidence: The coat of arms of the van der Beurze family depicts three purses ... and thereby gave both the family its name and gave rise to the word 'bourse'.
fix: The word's link to Bruges is a traditional account, not a documented fact. The National Bank of Belgium museum says the term referred to the square rather than the inn, and that the word spread from Antwerp. The Van der Beurze inn is dated to about 1285, and 1309 comes from a single secondary source. Reword to 'traditionally said to give the word bourse', and use c. 1285–1309.

text: Brugge, 1500 CE: Zwin silts up; trade moves to Antwerp.
evidence: The Zwin began to progressively silt up in the 13th century.
fix: The silting was gradual. It began in the 13th century, and the shift to Antwerp ran from the 1460s to the 1480s (revolts against Maximilian) and into the 16th century, with the Hanseatic kontor leaving in the 16th. Present 1500 as the approximate end of a long process, not a single event.

text: Budapest, 1241 CE: Destroyed by the Mongols.
evidence: Pest was destroyed in the 1241 Mongol invasion of Hungary, but was rebuilt shortly thereafter.
fix: Say that Pest was destroyed. Sources do not clearly show Buda being destroyed.

text: Budapest, 1541 CE: Ottoman conquest.
evidence: The Ottomans then took the city, and immediately organised the first Central European eyalet (province) with its capital in Buda.

text: Budapest, 1873 CE: Buda and Pest unite.
evidence: The city of Budapest was officially created on 17 November 1873 from a merger of the three neighboring cities of Pest, Buda and Óbuda.

text: Budapest, 1956 CE: Revolution crushed.
evidence: Soviet tanks entered the capital on the morning of 4 November, beginning the 'Operation Whirlwind' intervention.

sources.cite: Soviets put brutal end to Hungarian Revolution (history.com)

text: Buenos Aires, 1536 CE: First founding, soon abandoned.
evidence: Pedro de Mendoza founded Buenos Aires on February 2, 1536; the settlement was abandoned by 1541 and refounded in 1580 by Juan de Garay.

text: Buenos Aires, 1810 CE: May Revolution.
evidence: It took place from 18 to 25 May 1810, in Buenos Aires, capital of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata.

text: Bukhara, 1220 CE: Taken by Genghis Khan.
evidence: The siege of Bukhara took place in February 1220 and ended in a Mongol victory, with a force commanded by Genghis himself.

text: Bukhara, 1920 CE: Taken by the Red Army.
evidence: The war lasted between 28 August and 2 September 1920, ending in the defeat of the Emirate of Bukhara, which was replaced by the RSFSR-controlled Bukharan People's Soviet Republic.

text: Bukhara, 892 CE: Samanid capital.
evidence: Capital: Samarkand (819–892); Bukhara (892–999)

text: Byblos, 1104 CE: Taken by Crusaders.
evidence: With the Genoese Hugh Embriaco, Raymond also seized Gibelet.
fix: The 1104 date comes from a tourism timeline (28 April 1104), not a scholarly page. It is consistent with the Siege of Tripoli article.

text: Byblos, 1000 BCE: Ahiram's tomb carries an early Phoenician alphabet.
evidence: Most scholars have taken the Ahiram inscription to date from around 1000 B.C.E.
fix: Optionally say 'c. 1000 BCE, date disputed'. The article calls it the oldest witness to the Phoenician alphabet of considerable length.

text: Byblos, 2600 BCE: Ships cedar to Old Kingdom Egypt.
evidence: Reliefs in Sahure's pyramid complex show ships returning from Syria, perhaps from an expedition to obtain wood.
fix: The general claim holds: Old Kingdom Egypt imported Byblos cedar. I found no page that dates it exactly to 2600 BCE. The Palermo Stone claim of 40 ships under Sneferu was only in secondary retellings.

text: Cadiz, 1587 CE: Drake raids the harbour.
evidence: Drake sailed from Plymouth on 12 April 1587, reached the bay on 29 April, and the English withdrew at dawn on 1 May.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Singeing the King of Spain's Beard

text: Cadiz, 1717 CE: Wins the Americas trade monopoly from Seville.
evidence: The Casa de Contratación was founded in Seville in 1503 and later moved to Cádiz in 1717.

text: Cadiz, 1812 CE: Spain's liberal constitution written here.
evidence: The liberal Cortes drafted and ratified the Spanish Constitution of 1812, which established a constitutional monarchy.

text: Cadiz, 206 BCE: Joins Rome.
evidence: 206 BCE - Gades surrenders to the Romans under Scipio Africanus

text: Cahokia, 1050 CE: Sudden 'big bang' growth.
evidence: Around AD 1050 large earthen mounds were constructed and new forms of pottery styles, new kinds of stone tools, new architectural elements, and neighborhood planning appeared. This rapid process of growth in size and complexity at Cahokia is called "the big bang".

sources.cite: Cahokia (ancient Cahokia and the Mississippian culture) (mythicmississippi.illinois.edu)

text: Cairo, 1168 CE: Fustat burned to keep it from Crusaders.
evidence: Shawar ordered the burning of his own capital city, Fustat, just so that the enemy could not have it.
fix: Optional: soften to 'Fustat was set on fire'. Some sources say the burning was limited and the city continued after 1168.

text: Cairo, 1348 CE: Black Death.
evidence: It reached Cairo in September 1348, when the city was the largest in the Middle East and the Mediterranean world.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Black Death in the Middle East

text: Cairo, 1517 CE: Ottoman conquest.
evidence: Cairo fell on 27–30 January 1517, and the Mamluk Sultanate was absorbed into the expanding Ottoman Empire after its last sultan, Tuman Bay II, was executed.

text: Cairo, 1798 CE: Napoleon's army arrives.
evidence: The French defeated the Mamluks at the Battle of the Pyramids on 21 July 1798, and Bonaparte entered Cairo on the twenty-fourth.

text: Cairo, 1952 CE: Revolution ends the monarchy.
evidence: Wikipedia's infobox lists the 1952 coup as the event that ended Muhammad Ali dynasty rule (the search summary's wording, not a verbatim page sentence)
fix: Optionally add that the Republic was formally declared on 18 June 1953. Farouk abdicated in July 1952.

text: Cairo, 969 CE: Founded by the Fatimids.
evidence: A general under the command of the Fatimid Sultan Al-Muizz li-Din Allah, Al-Siqilli founded Cairo to become the centre from which Al-Muizz and his successors would rule the Islamic world.

sources.cite: Jawahar al Siqilli the Italy born commander who built Cairo Al Azhar mosque (english.alarabiya.net)

text: Cairo, 970 CE: Al-Azhar founded.
evidence: Jawhar, the Sicilian commander of the army sent by the Fāṭimid caliph-imām al-Muʿizz li-Dīn Allah, founded this mosque on Saturday, 24 Jumādā I 359/April 4, 970 ce.

text: Caral, 1994 CE: Ruth Shady begins excavations.
evidence: She has worked at the Caral site from 1994 onwards.

text: Carthage, 439 CE: Vandal capital.
evidence: Wikipedia's Vandal Kingdom infobox lists Hippo Regius (435–439) Carthage (439–534) as the capital.

text: Carthage, 533 CE: Retaken by Byzantium.
evidence: Gelimer's plan to encircle the Roman army nearly worked, but Belisarius routed the Vandals at Ad Decimum (13 September 533) and took Carthage.

text: Carthage, 698 CE: Destroyed by the Umayyads.
evidence: Fearing a Byzantine comeback, the Umayyads deliberately wrecked the city after taking it in 698, tearing down the walls, cutting the water supply and making the harbours unusable, and moved their administrative center to Tunis.

text: Carthage, 146 BCE: Razed by Rome.
evidence: The final Roman hammer blow came in the spring of 146 BCE when they launched an all-out attack on Carthage.

text: Carthage, 218 BCE: Hannibal marches on Italy.
evidence: Wikipedia gives the crossing as running from May/July to late September 218 BC.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Hannibal's crossing of the Alps

text: Carthage, 264 BCE: First Punic War begins.
evidence: The war began in 264 BC with the Romans gaining a foothold on Sicily at Messana.

text: Carthage, 29 BCE: Refounded as a Roman colony.
evidence: Julius Caesar's planned veteran settlement was prevented from completion by his assassination in 44 BC.
fix: Caesar planned and began the refounding in 44 BCE (Wikipedia says he rebuilt it between 49 and 44 BC). Augustus carried it out from about 29 BCE. Reword as 'refounded as a Roman colony, planned by Caesar in 44 BCE and carried out under Augustus from about 29 BCE'.

text: Chan Chan, 1470 CE: Inca conquest.
evidence: After the Inca conquered the Chimú around 1470 AD, Chan Chan fell into decline.

text: Chennai, 1639 CE: Fort St George founded.
evidence: Thanks to negotiations led by Francis Day with ruler of Chandragiri in 1639, English succeeded in purchasing a piece of coastal land.
fix: Optionally note that the fort was completed on 23 April 1644.

text: Chennai, 1746 CE: Taken by the French.
evidence: The Battle of Madras took place on 7–9 September 1746 and ended in a French victory over the British East India Company garrison.
fix: Optionally note that the French returned Madras under the 1748 Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle.

text: Chichén Itzá, 1000 CE: Pyramid of Kukulcán completed.
evidence: The Maya built it sometime between the 8th and 12th centuries CE, and it served as a temple to Kukulcán.
fix: No source gives 1000 CE as a firm completion date. Say 'built in stages, c. 8th–12th century CE; the final stage is tentatively dated about 900/1000 CE'.

text: Cholula, 1519 CE: Cholula massacre by Cortés's forces.
evidence: Wikipedia gives about 6,000 killed in under two hours, per Gómara.

text: Cholula, 1594 CE: Church built on top of the pyramid.
evidence: built between May 1574 and August 1575 and consecrated on March 25, 1629
fix: Sources disagree. Some say a hermitage or church was begun in 1594. Wikipedia dates the church to 1574–1575 and its consecration to 1629. Say 'late 16th century' or 'begun 1594 per some sources'.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Iglesia de Nuestra Señora de los Remedios, Cholula

text: Cholula, 200 BCE: Great Pyramid construction under way.
evidence: Built: c. 3rd century BC, Abandoned: c. 8th century AD

text: Cologne, 1248 CE: Cathedral begun.
evidence: Construction of Cologne Cathedral began in 1248 but was halted in 1473, unfinished.

text: Cologne, 1880 CE: Cathedral finished.
evidence: the edifice was completed to its original Medieval plan in 1880

text: Cologne, 1942 CE: 1,000-bomber raid.
evidence: The first thousand raid by the RAF was conducted on Cologne during the night of 30–31 May 1942.

text: Córdoba, Spain, 1013 CE: Sacked by Berber troops.
evidence: Córdoba surrendered to the Berbers in May 1013, and the North Africans sacked the city, killing many inhabitants.

text: Córdoba, Spain, 1236 CE: Taken by Castile.
evidence: The siege of Córdoba was a successful investment by the forces of Ferdinand III, king of Castile and León, marking the end of the Islamic rule over the city that had begun in 711.

text: Córdoba, Spain, 785 CE: Great Mosque begun.
evidence: the mosque was constructed in 785 on the orders of Abd al-Rahman I, founder of the Islamic Emirate of Córdoba

text: Córdoba, Spain, 929 CE: Caliphate proclaimed.
evidence: the caliphate's founding dates to the self-proclamation of Umayyad emir Abd ar-Rahman III as caliph in January 929

text: Ctesiphon, 637 CE: Taken by Arab armies.
evidence: the Rashidun army, under Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, took the city after a two-month siege

text: Cusco, 1438 CE: Pachacuti rebuilds it as imperial capital.
evidence: 1438 Pachacunti Inca Yupanqui begins a rebuilding programme in the Inca capital of Cuzco.
fix: Optional: say the rebuilding is traditional. Wikipedia's Cusco article says archaeology shows slower growth that began before Pachacuti.

text: Cusco, 1533 CE: Taken by Pizarro.
evidence: the Spanish entered Cuzco on 15 November 1533

text: Cusco, 1650 CE: Earthquake.
evidence: a significant quake that struck Cuzco on March 31, 1650, measuring around 7.5 on the Richter scale

text: Cusco, 1950 CE: Earthquake.
evidence: El terremoto del 21 de mayo de 1950 dañó más de un 50 % los edificios del Cusco y ocasionó 394 víctimas entre muertos y heridos.
