text: Damascus, 1401 CE: Sacked by Timur.
evidence: The siege ran from December 1400 – March 1401, and it is also known as the Sack of Damascus.

text: Damascus, 1516 CE: Ottoman conquest.
evidence: reached the outskirts of Damascus on 27 September 1516, entering the city center on 3 October

text: Damascus, 2011 CE: Syrian civil war begins.
evidence: The article gives the start date as 15 March 2011 and says the regime's lethal crackdown turned the uprising into an armed conflict.

text: Damascus, 634 CE: Taken by Arab Muslim armies.
evidence: The Wikipedia article on the siege gives 21 August to 19 September 634, and Damascus was the first major city of the Eastern Roman Empire to fall in the Muslim conquest of Syria.
fix: Some sources put the capture in 635, and the Byzantines briefly retook the city before Yarmuk in 636, but Wikipedia gives 634.

text: Damascus, 661 CE: Becomes the Umayyad capital.
evidence: In 661 Muʿāwiyah, the first Umayyad caliph, established his court in the Syrian capital and founded a dār al-imārah (centre of government) there.

text: Damascus, 715 CE: Great Umayyad Mosque completed.
evidence: Wikipedia lists Completed: 715 CE with al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik as founder.
fix: Optional: one source says Sulayman finished the work after al-Walid died in 715, so the exact completion year varies slightly.

text: Damascus, 732 BCE: Conquered by Assyria.
evidence: King Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria seizing Damascus, executing Rezin, King of the Arameans, and deporting the Aramaean inhabitants (listed under 732 BCE, marked as a probable date).

text: Delhi, 1206 CE: Delhi Sultanate founded.
evidence: The Wikipedia infobox lists his coronation as 25 June 1206 at Qasr-e-Humayun in Lahore, and his reign as running until 4 November 1210.
fix: Aibak was crowned in Lahore, not Delhi, but 1206 is the standard founding date of the Sultanate.

text: Delhi, 1398 CE: Sacked by Timur.
evidence: The sack of Delhi took place on 17–20 December 1398.

text: Delhi, 1639 CE: Shah Jahan begins Shahjahanabad.
evidence: Google Arts & Culture says construction of the Lal Qila began in 1639 and ended in 1648.
fix: Wikipedia gives 1638–1649 for the walled city's construction and 1648 as the official naming year, so 1639 for the start is right but not the only date given.

text: Delhi, 1739 CE: Sacked by Nader Shah.
evidence: Nader entered the city on 20 March 1739 and took up residence in the Red Fort. In retaliation Nader Shah ordered mass executions and sack of the city.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Nader Shah's invasion of India

text: Delhi, 1857 CE: Rebellion crushed by the British.
evidence: Britannica gives the siege as June 8, 1857 - September 21, 1857, and says the siege extinguished Indian dreams of re-creating the rule of the Mughal Empire.
fix: Optionally say 'Delhi recaptured by the British' because the wider rebellion continued into 1858.

text: Delhi, 1931 CE: New Delhi inaugurated.
evidence: The city that was later dubbed "Lutyens' Delhi" was inaugurated in ceremonies beginning on 10 February 1931 by Lord Irwin, the Viceroy.

text: Dilmun (Qal'at al-Bahrain), 2000 BCE: Peak of the Gulf trade in copper and pearls.
evidence: Dilmun flourished c. 2000 bce, centred on Bahrain Island in the Persian Gulf; copper and a variety of other goods, including stone beads, precious stones, pearls, dates, and vegetables, were shipped to Sumer and Babylonia.

text: Dublin, 1916 CE: Easter Rising.
evidence: The Rising began on Easter Monday, 24 April 1916 and lasted for six days.

text: Dublin, 841 CE: Viking longphort founded.
evidence: Dublin appears to have been founded twice by the Vikings. The first foundation was as a longphort where the Scandinavians overwintered from 841AD onwards.

text: Ebla, 1974 CE: Royal archive found.
evidence: The first cuneiform tablets were found in 1974 in Room L.2586, a small group of 42 lenticular tablets. The room holding the royal archive was discovered on the first of October, 1975.
fix: Change to 1975 for the royal archive (Great Archive L.2769). 1974 was only a small first group of tablets.

sources.cite: The Archives of Ebla: A Primer (iaassyriology.com)

text: Ephesus, 1304 CE: Taken by the Turks.
evidence: Sasa Bey of the Beylik of Menteshe and the sons of Aydin together took Ephesus in October 1304.

text: Ephesus, 262 CE: Sacked by Goths.
evidence: In 262 A.D., the Goths destroyed Ephesus, including the Temple of Artemis.
fix: Optional: note that some sources, including Wikipedia's Ephesus article, give 263.

text: Ephesus, 431 CE: Council of Ephesus.
evidence: The First Council of Ephesus (431) is known as the Third Ecumenical Council and was convened over the Nestorian controversy.

text: Ephesus, 54 CE: Paul preaches here.
evidence: Paul in Ephesus (Acts 18:23-19:41, 52-55 AD)
fix: 54 CE falls inside the usual 52-55 range, but the stay lasted about three years. Consider showing it as 52-55 CE.

text: Ephesus, 356 BCE: Temple of Artemis burned.
evidence: The version of the temple that stood until 356 BC was burned down by an arsonist, popularly identified as Herostratus.

text: Erbil, 331 BCE: Battle of Gaugamela nearby.
evidence: Gaugamela, a village on the banks of the river Bumodus, north of Arbela (modern-day Erbil).
fix: The exact battle site is still debated, so keep the wording as 'nearby'.

text: Fatehpur Sikri, 1571 CE: Akbar begins building.
evidence: The UCLA South Asia page dates the commencement of the new ceremonial capital to 1571.
fix: Some sources give 1569 or 1572 as the start, so 1571 is the most common date but not the only one. I did not see the exact UCLA sentence, so this quote is the search summary's paraphrase.

text: Fatehpur Sikri, 1575 CE: Ibadat Khana debates between religions.
evidence: The Ibādat Khāna (House of Worship) was a meeting house built in 1575 CE by the Mughal Emperor Akbar.
fix: The hall was ordered built in January 1575 and finished in 1576. Debates began shortly after that.

text: Fatehpur Sikri, 1585 CE: Court moves to Lahore.
evidence: Akbar abandoned Fatehpur Sikri to fight against the Afghan tribes and choose a new capital, Lahore.
fix: The court left in 1585. Sources say the city was fully abandoned later, by about 1610.

text: Fez, Morocco, 1912 CE: French protectorate.
evidence: The Treaty of Fez was signed on 30 March 1912 and established the French protectorate over Morocco.

text: Fez, Morocco, 859 CE: Al-Qarawiyyin founded.
evidence: Wikipedia gives 857–859; many popular sources say Al-Fihri founded the University of Al-Qarawiyyin in Fes, Morocco in 859 CE.

text: Florence, 1252 CE: Gold florin first minted.
evidence: Florence began minting it in 1252.

text: Florence, 1348 CE: Black Death.
evidence: In March 1348, the plague reached Florence, lasting until July.

text: Florence, 1436 CE: Brunelleschi's dome completed.
evidence: Building work began on 7 August 1420 and the dome was finally completed 16 years later; the cathedral was consecrated by Pope Eugenius IV on 25 March 1436.

text: Florence, 1865 CE: Capital of Italy for six years.
evidence: Florence served as Italy's capital from 1865 to 1871, although it lasted only six years.

text: Gao, 1464 CE: Sunni Ali makes Songhai an empire.
evidence: In 1464, when Ali succeeded the fourteenth si, Sulaiman Dama, Gao was still a tributary province under the Mali empire; Ali transformed the relatively small state into an empire.

text: Gao, 1591 CE: Battle of Tondibi nearby.
evidence: The Battle of Tondibi was fought on 13 March 1591 near Gao in what is now Mali, and it was a decisive Moroccan victory.

text: Genoa, 1284 CE: Crushes Pisa at Meloria.
evidence: The Battle of Meloria was a decisive Genoese naval victory over Pisa on August 5–6, 1284, near the islet of Meloria in the Ligurian Sea.

text: Genoa, 1557 CE: Its bankers lend to Spain's Philip II.
fix: The pages found list Spanish defaults in 1557, 1560, 1575 and 1596 and describe Genoese bankers as Philip II's lenders. None says the Genoese lent to him in 1557 specifically. Either find a source or reword to the 1557 default, after which Genoese bankers replaced the Fuggers.

sources.cite: Poor Fuggers — is Spain bust again? (globalcapital.com)

text: Great Pyramid of Giza, 1303 CE: Earthquake loosens casing stones, later taken for Cairo.
evidence: The outer casing stone blocks fell down completely in 1303 strong earthquake.
fix: A source supports the 1303 earthquake, but says the casing fell down, not that it was merely loosened. A separate source says the stone was removed as building material. No page found ties the removed stone to Cairo. Reword to: casing stones fell in the 1303 earthquake and were later removed as building stone.

sources.cite: Heritage Science (Springer Open) article on the Great Pyramid, figure 7 (heritagesciencejournal.springeropen.com)

text: Granada, 1238 CE: Nasrid capital; Alhambra begun.
evidence: The complex was begun in 1238 by Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar, the first Nasrid emir and founder of the Emirate of Granada.

text: Granada, 1492 CE: Surrenders to Ferdinand and Isabella.
evidence: Muhammad XI of Granada (King Boabdil) surrendered the Emirate of Granada, the city of Granada, and the Alhambra palace to the Castilian forces (2 January 1492).

text: Great Zimbabwe, 1871 CE: European explorers wrongly credit it to outsiders.
evidence: Mauch reported on the archaeological ruins of Great Zimbabwe in 1871 during his search for the biblical land of Ophir. He believed the ruins had once been the palace of the Queen of Sheba.

text: Guangzhou, 1757 CE: Canton System begins.
evidence: The policy arose in 1757 as a response to a perceived political and commercial threat from abroad.

text: Guangzhou, 1841 CE: British attack in the Opium War.
evidence: Charles Elliot, Gordon Bremer and Thomas Herbert took five Qing forts and 123 guns.

text: Guangzhou, 879 CE: Huang Chao's rebels massacre foreign merchants.
evidence: it was also the foreign merchants who were attacked at Canton by the troops of Huang Ch'ao in 879

text: Gyeongju, 1238 CE: Mongols burn Hwangnyongsa pagoda.
evidence: The nine-story wooden pagoda was destroyed by fire during the Mongolian invasion in 1238.

text: Gyeongju, 668 CE: Silla unifies Korea.
evidence: Munmu was the first ruler ever to see the Korean Peninsula unified
fix: 668 is the date Goguryeo fell. Optionally add that Silla controlled only the peninsula south of the Taedong River by 676, and that Balhae remained in the north.

text: Gyeongju, 935 CE: Silla surrenders to Goryeo.
evidence: Gyeongsun, the last king of Silla, handed his kingdom to Goryeo's founder Taejo in 935, which ended the Silla dynasty.

text: Hamadān, 550 BCE: Taken by Cyrus the Great.
evidence: In 550 BCE, the Median capital, Ecbatana, was conquered by the Persian leader Cyrus the Great, marking the beginning of the Achaemenid Empire.

text: Hamburg, 1189 CE: Free trading rights; Hanseatic hub.
evidence: The surviving charter is dated 7 May 1189, but it actually originated in the 1360s, during a dispute between Hamburg and the Archbishop of Bremen over duties on the Elbe.
fix: The 1189 grant was duty-free passage on the Lower Elbe, given by Barbarossa, reportedly orally. The surviving charter is a later forgery or reworking. The 1189 grant did not make Hamburg a Hanseatic hub. Reword to 'traditional date of Barbarossa's duty-free Elbe privilege (Port of Hamburg's birthday)'. I found no source in this search for the Hanseatic part.

text: Hamburg, 1842 CE: Great Fire.
evidence: The 1842 Great Fire of Hamburg broke out in the early hours of 5 May and burned until 8 May.

text: Hamburg, 1943 CE: Firestorm.
evidence: The key night was 27/28 July 1943, when a firestorm killed more than 40,000 people in and around Hamburg.

sources.cite: Operation Gomorrah: The First of the Firestorms (nationalww2museum.org)

text: Hangzhou, 1132 CE: Becomes the Southern Song capital.
evidence: Hangzhou was chosen as the new capital of the Southern Song dynasty in 1132, when most of northern China had been conquered by the Jurchens (paraphrase of the search summary, not a verbatim quote).
fix: Optionally note that other pages give 1138 for Lin'an's formal designation as capital.

text: Hangzhou, 1276 CE: Surrenders to the Mongols.
evidence: In February 1276, Grand Empress Dowager Xie carried the five-year-old emperor out of Lin'an and into the Mongol camp, where she too surrendered (as summarized by the search).

text: Hangzhou, 1861 CE: Taken by the Taiping.
evidence: Dec 29 Taipings take Hangzhou (1861 timeline entry, as summarized by the search).
fix: Optionally say Dec 1861. The Taiping also took the city briefly in March 1860.

sources.cite: TaipingRebellion.com 太平天囯 Tai Ping Tian Guo (taipingrebellion.com)

text: Hanoi, 1010 CE: Lý dynasty capital.
evidence: Lý Thái Tổ set up the capital in 1010 in the Đại La area, which became central Hanoi, and named it Thăng Long (paraphrase of the search summary).

text: Hanoi, 1258 CE: Mongol attack repelled.
evidence: The 1258 campaign is listed as a Mongol victory: the Trần court left the capital and the Mongols captured it, then withdrew to pursue the Song (paraphrase of the search summary).
fix: Reword to something like 'Mongols take and sack Thăng Long, then withdraw'. Vietnam's successful repulsions of the Mongols came in 1285 and 1288.

text: Hanoi, 1954 CE: Capital of North Vietnam.
evidence: The French lost at Dien Bien Phu on May 7, 1954, and shortly thereafter Hanoi became the capital of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam (North Vietnam) (paraphrase of the search summary).

text: Harappa, 1856 CE: Bricks hauled off for the railway.
evidence: A British road-engineer, named William Brunton (spelled 'Bounton' on the page), dug into the remains in 1856 (paraphrase of the search summary).
fix: Optionally say 'mid-1850s'. Some Wikipedia-derived sources give 1857, and the bricks went to the Lahore–Multan line as ballast.

sources.cite: Harappa heritage site listing (Department of Archaeology and Museums, Pakistan) (doam.gov.pk)

text: Harappa, 1921 CE: Excavations begin.
evidence: Excavation proper started in January 1921 on Mounds F and AB, under Rai Bahadur Daya Ram Sahni (paraphrase of the search summary).

text: Hattusa, 1180 BCE: Burned and abandoned.
evidence: Signs of final destruction by fire have been noted, but this destruction probably occurred after the city had already been abandoned by the Hittite royal family, elites, and state apparatus.
fix: Say the city was abandoned c. 1180 BCE. The fire probably came after the court had left, so "burned and abandoned" in that order is misleading.

text: Hattusa, 1259 BCE: Peace treaty with Egypt, the oldest known.
evidence: Wikipedia describes it as the oldest known surviving peace treaty (summary of the page; search snippet, not a verbatim quote).
fix: Optionally say "oldest surviving". An earlier Ebla–Abarsal agreement may be older.

text: Hattusa, 1274 BCE: Hittites fight Egypt at Kadesh.
evidence: The Battle of Kadesh took place around 1274 BC (summary of the page; search snippet, not a verbatim quote). One other source gives 1275 BCE.

text: Hattusa, 1650 BCE: Hattusili I makes it the Hittite capital.
evidence: Britannica gives Hattusili I's reign as c. 1650–c. 1620 bc (summary of the page; search snippet, not a verbatim quote). He took his name after transferring his capital to Hattusa.
fix: Wording only: sources differ on whether he moved the capital from Kussara or from Neša, and on whether Labarna did the move.

text: Havana, 1762 CE: Taken by the British.
evidence: The British captured Havana during the Seven Years' War in 1762 (summary of the page; search snippet, not a verbatim quote). The city was returned to Spain afterward in exchange for the Floridas.

text: Havana, 1898 CE: USS Maine explodes in the harbour.
evidence: The USS Maine exploded and sank in Havana harbor on the night of February 15, 1898 (summary of the page; search snippet, not a verbatim quote).

text: Havana, 1959 CE: Revolution takes power.
evidence: The Triumph of the Revolution is the historical term for the flight of Fulgencio Batista on January 1, 1959, and the capture of Havana by the 26 July Movement on January 8 (summary of the page; search snippet, not a verbatim quote).

text: Hedeby, 1050 CE: Burned by Harald Hardrada.
evidence: Hedeby in Jutland is sacked by King Harald Hardrada of Norway, during the course of a conflict with Sweyn II of Denmark.
fix: Optionally say "sacked and burned". One source hedges that Harald "probably" did it.

text: Hedeby, 1066 CE: Sacked by Slavs.
evidence: Sacked by Polabian Slavs (1066)

text: Hedeby, 808 CE: Grows under King Godfred.
evidence: In 808, Godfred destroyed the Slavic trading centre of Reric and took its merchants with him to Hedeby.

text: Thonis-Heracleion, 2000 CE: Found by divers in Abu Qir Bay.
evidence: In 2000, Goddio discovered the city of Thonis-Heracleion 7 km off the Egyptian shore in Aboukir Bay.

text: Herāt, 1221 CE: Destroyed by the Mongols.
evidence: Iranica dates the fall of the city to June-July 1222 after a siege of about seven months.
fix: The Mongols first took Herat in 1221. After a revolt, the city was razed and its people massacred in 1222. Change the date to 1222, or reword to 'Mongols take Herat; razed after revolt in 1222'.

text: Herāt, 1405 CE: Shah Rukh's Timurid capital.
evidence: Shah Rukh's reign is given as beginning 20 February 1405, with Herat as his capital.

text: Isfahan, 1051 CE: Seljuk capital.
evidence: 1051: Tughril's forces besiege Isfahan and the city becomes the Seljuk Empire's capital.

text: Isfahan, 1387 CE: Timur massacres the city.
evidence: Isfahan surrendered, then rebelled over Timurid taxes, and Timur retook it and ordered mass killings (70,000–200,000 estimated).

text: Isfahan, 1598 CE: Shah Abbas's Safavid capital.
evidence: The Met dates Shah Abbas's move of the capital to Isfahan to 1597–98.

sources.cite: Shah 'Abbas and the Arts of Isfahan (metmuseum.org)

text: Isfahan, 1722 CE: Afghan siege and famine.
evidence: The city was soon struck by famine, which forced Soltan Hoseyn to surrender on 21 October 1722.

text: Istanbul, 1204 CE: Sacked by the Fourth Crusade.
evidence: The sack of Constantinople took place in April 1204 and marked the culmination of the Fourth Crusade.

text: Istanbul, 1453 CE: Taken by Mehmed II.
evidence: The city fell to Mehmed II's forces on May 29, 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire.

text: Istanbul, 1923 CE: Ankara becomes Türkiye's capital.
evidence: The bill was accepted in the Assembly with a great majority on 13 October 1923.

text: Istanbul, 330 CE: Refounded by Constantine as capital.
evidence: The city was solemnly dedicated as New Rome, Constantinople, the city of Constantine, on May 11, 330.

text: Istanbul, 537 CE: Hagia Sophia completed.
evidence: Construction of the current Hagia Sophia began in February 532 AD and finished in December 537 AD.

sources.cite: Hagia Sophia: when was it built (hagiasophia.com)

text: Istanbul, 541 CE: Plague of Justinian.
evidence: The plague reached Roman Egypt in 541, spread around the Mediterranean until 544... Most sources date its arrival in the capital to 542.
fix: The plague began in Egypt in 541 but reached Constantinople in 542. Change the Istanbul event to 542, or say 'Plague of Justinian reaches the city, 542'.

text: Jerusalem, 1099 CE: Crusaders storm the city.
evidence: The siege of Jerusalem from 7 June 1099 to 15 July 1099 marked the successful end of the First Crusade.

text: Jerusalem, 1187 CE: Saladin retakes it.
evidence: Saladin's forces besieged Jerusalem from September 20 and took the city on October 2, 1187, after the crusader garrison surrendered.

text: Jerusalem, 1517 CE: Ottoman rule begins.
evidence: Ottoman Jerusalem, 1517-1918
fix: Optional: some sources say the city submitted in late 1516, before Cairo fell in 1517.

text: Jerusalem, 1948 CE: Divided after the 1948 war.
evidence: The City Line divided Jerusalem between Israel (in the western part) and Jordan (in the eastern part, including the Old City and the Temple Mount) for 19 years.

text: Jerusalem, 1967 CE: Six-Day War.
evidence: Israel captured East Jerusalem on the third day of the Six Day War.

sources.cite: Today in History: One Jerusalem (CBS News) (cbsnews.com)

text: Jerusalem, 638 CE: Taken by Caliph Umar's armies.
evidence: Caliph Umar traveled to Jerusalem in person to receive the submission of the city, which Wikipedia dates to 637 or 638.
fix: Optional: say 637/638, since sources differ and academic sources tend to prefer 638.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, First Muslim conquest of Jerusalem

text: Jerusalem, 691 CE: Dome of the Rock completed.
evidence: The shrine was first finished in 691–92 CE on Abd al-Malik's orders, during the Second Fitna.

text: Jerusalem, 70 CE: Destroyed by Rome.
evidence: The Wikipedia-derived text gives August 30, 70 CE as the end of the siege, with the Temple burned, and says the conquest of the city was complete on September 8, 70 CE.

text: Jerusalem, 1000 BCE: David makes it his capital (by tradition).
evidence: According to the Bible, the Israelite history of the city began in c. 1000 BCE.

text: Jerusalem, 516 BCE: Second Temple completed.
evidence: Wikipedia's infobox lists c. 516 BCE for the original structure.

text: Jerusalem, 587 BCE: Destroyed by Babylon; exile begins.
evidence: Nebuchadnezzar returned, defeated the Egyptians, and again besieged Jerusalem, resulting in the city's destruction in 587 BCE.
fix: Optionally write 587/586 BCE, since sources split between the two years.

text: Kaifeng, 1127 CE: Taken by the Jurchen Jin.
evidence: The Jin captured Bianjing, the Northern Song capital (present-day Kaifeng), in 1127.

text: Kaifeng, 1642 CE: Drowned when the Yellow River dikes are cut.
evidence: In October 1642, the Ming governor of Kaifeng ordered the Yellow River's dikes broken to wash away the peasant rebels under Li Zicheng, who had besieged the city for about six months.

text: Kaifeng, 960 CE: Northern Song capital.
evidence: After the Chenqiao Mutiny in 960, Zhao Kuangyin became the first Northern Song emperor, and Dongjing (present-day Kaifeng) was designated as the imperial capital.

text: Kairouan, 1057 CE: Sacked by the Banu Hilal.
evidence: The city of Kairouan was looted by the Banu Hilal in 1057 after it was abandoned by the Zirids.

text: Kairouan, 670 CE: Founded by Uqba ibn Nafi.
evidence: Wikipedia's entry lists the founding as 670 CE, with Uqba ibn Nafi named as founder.

text: Kano, 1903 CE: Taken by the British.
evidence: Colonel Thomas Morland's force reached Kano after leaving Zaria in late January. The fighting began on 3 February (1903).

text: Karakorum, 1235 CE: Ögedei builds its walls.
evidence: Ogedei Khan later built a wall around the entire city in 1236.
fix: Wikipedia, citing the Yuanshi and the 1342 inscription, dates the wall to 1236. Worldhistory.org says Ögedei ordered the walled capital in 1235. Change the date to 1236, or say "ordered 1235, walls built 1236".

text: Karakorum, 1254 CE: William of Rubruck visits.
evidence: He reached Möngke's mobile court on 27 December 1253 and the capital, Karakorum in present-day Mongolia, on 5 April 1254.

text: Karakorum, 1388 CE: Razed by Ming troops.
evidence: Conflicts between the Ming and the so-called Northern Yuan court finally resulted in the destruction of Qaraqorum in 1388.
fix: Some sources, such as the Wikipedia article on Uskhal Khan, give 1380 instead. 1388 is the more common date.

text: Kilwa Kisiwani, 1331 CE: Ibn Battuta visits.
evidence: Ibn Battuta visited the court in 1331 and spoke very highly of the sultan as a humble, generous and pious ruler.

text: Kilwa Kisiwani, 1505 CE: Sacked by the Portuguese.
evidence: The sack of Kilwa took place on 24 July 1505 under Francisco de Almeida.

text: Knossos, 1900 CE: Arthur Evans starts digging.
evidence: Evans completed negotiations for the purchase of the site in 1900, and excavation began, with the assistance of experienced field archaeologist Duncan Mackenzie.

text: Knossos, 1700 BCE: Palace rebuilt after an earthquake.
evidence: The palace was destroyed for the first time along with the other Protopalatial palaces of Crete in 1700 BC, probably by a large earthquake or foreign invaders. The New Palace was immediately rebuilt, becoming larger and more imposing.
fix: The cause is not certain. "Probably an earthquake" would be safer wording. One source puts the rebuilding nearer 1650.

text: Kolkata, 1756 CE: Taken by the Nawab of Bengal.
evidence: Siraj ud-Daulah aimed to seize Calcutta to punish the company for the unauthorised construction of fortifications at Fort William. Siraj ud-Daulah caught the Company unprepared and won a decisive victory.

text: Kolkata, 1757 CE: Battle of Plassey; Company rule begins.
evidence: British rule in India is conventionally described as having begun in 1757.

text: Kolkata, 1911 CE: Capital moves to Delhi.
evidence: On December 12, 1911, at Coronation Park in Delhi, he announced that the seat of the Government of India would move from Calcutta to Delhi.
fix: The announcement was in 1911, but the move itself took about 20 years to carry out. New Delhi was inaugurated in 1931. Consider wording it as 'Capital move to Delhi announced'.

sources.cite: King George V's Announcement of Delhi as Capital Stunned Many (thequint.com)

text: Kolkata, 1943 CE: Bengal famine.
evidence: The Bengal famine of 1943 struck Bengal Province and Orissa Province in British India during World War II.

text: Kraków, 1241 CE: Burned by the Mongols.
evidence: On 31 March 1241 the Mongols set Kraków on fire; the next day they left the city, heading towards Silesia.

text: Kraków, 1596 CE: Capital moves to Warsaw.
evidence: Sigismund initially stayed in Warsaw only temporarily while the castle was rebuilt, and in 1611 he moved there for good.
fix: Sigismund III moved his court to Warsaw in 1596, after a fire at Wawel. Kraków stayed the formal capital and coronation city, and the king settled in Warsaw permanently in 1611. Say 'Royal court moves to Warsaw' instead of 'Capital moves'.

text: Kyiv, 1240 CE: Sacked by the Mongols.
evidence: 28 November – 6 December 1240, a Mongol victory; Kiev plundered, most civilians slaughtered.

text: Kyiv, 1941 CE: Babyn Yar massacre.
evidence: 33,771 Jews were killed by Einsatzgruppe C in just two days, 29–30 September 1941.

text: Kyiv, 988 CE: Volodymyr's baptism of Rus'.
evidence: The mass baptism of Kyiv's citizens is dated to 1 August 988.
fix: Some sources date Volodymyr's own baptism to December 987, and the place (Kyiv or Chersonese) is debated. 988 is the conventional date for the baptism of Rus'.

text: Kyoto, 1467 CE: Ōnin War burns much of the city.
evidence: Per Wikipedia's summary, most of Kyoto destroyed, and the war marked the start of the Sengoku period.

text: Kyoto, 1868 CE: Emperor moves to Tokyo.
evidence: Historians generally treat this second trip (1869) as the de facto relocation of the capital; no edict declaring the capital's relocation was ever issued.
fix: The emperor first visited Tokyo in late 1868 and returned to Kyoto. He moved there permanently in 1869 (Edo Castle, 9 May 1869). Change the year to 1869, or say 'moves to Tokyo 1868–69'.

text: Kyoto, 794 CE: Heian-kyō becomes capital.
evidence: Emperor Kanmu established Heian-kyō in 794 on the site of modern Kyoto.

text: Lahore, 1186 CE: Ghurid conquest.
evidence: Lahore was finally captured by the Ghurids in 1186, while Khusrau-Malik and his sons Malikshah and Bahram-Shah were taken to Ghur and imprisoned.

text: Lahore, 1585 CE: Akbar's capital.
evidence: Akbar stayed in the Fort for fourteen years at a stretch from 1585 to 1599.

sources.cite: Lahore As It Once Was: Fortress At The Nerve Centre Of An Empire (thefridaytimes.com)

text: Lahore, 1799 CE: Ranjit Singh's Sikh capital.
evidence: Wikipedia's infobox lists Gujranwala (1799–1802); Lahore (1802–1849).
fix: Ranjit Singh captured Lahore in 1799, but the Sikh capital was Gujranwala until 1802. Lahore became the capital in 1802. Say 'Ranjit Singh takes Lahore' for 1799, or date the capital to 1802.

text: Lahore, 1947 CE: Partition violence.
evidence: Riots broke out in Lahore in March 1947, and the violence drove an exodus of Hindus and Sikhs from the city.

sources.cite: Lahore @ Partition — Violence, Cross-Migration, and Regeneration 1947-1961 (dawn.com)

text: Lima, 1746 CE: Earthquake and tsunami.
evidence: The 1746 Lima–Callao earthquake struck on 28 October; Lima was almost completely destroyed, and the subsequent tsunami devastated the port city of Callao.

text: Lima, 1821 CE: Independence declared.
evidence: On July 28, 1821, José de San Martín officially declared Peru's independence from Spain.

text: Lisbon, 1147 CE: Taken from the Moors.
evidence: The city surrendered on 25 October 1147.

text: Lisbon, 1497 CE: Da Gama sails for India.
evidence: Vasco da Gama left Lisbon on 8 July 1497, with four ships.

text: Lisbon, 1755 CE: Earthquake, tsunami and fire.
evidence: The quake, combined with fires and a tsunami, almost completely destroyed Lisbon and adjoining areas.

text: London, 1066 CE: William the Conqueror crowned.
evidence: William was crowned at Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Coronations of William the Conqueror and Matilda

text: London, 1348 CE: Black Death.
evidence: Robert of Avesbury places the arrival on, or around, the feast of All Saints (1 November) 1348.

text: London, 1666 CE: Great Fire.
evidence: The Great Fire of London burned for several days in September 1666, starting on Sunday, September 2, 1666 at the king's baker's house on Pudding Lane.

text: London, 1851 CE: Great Exhibition.
evidence: The Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations ran in Hyde Park from May to October 1851.

text: London, 1940 CE: The Blitz.
evidence: On 7 September 1940, about 300 German bombers hit London, beginning 57 consecutive nights of bombing.

text: London, 61 CE: Burned in Boudica's revolt.
evidence: Boudica's army defeated a detachment of the Legio IX Hispana and burned both Londinium and Verulamium.

text: London, 886 CE: Alfred the Great reoccupies it.
evidence: The taking of London in 885 or 886.

text: Lübeck, 1356 CE: First general Hanseatic diet.
evidence: The first meeting of the Diet took place on 2 February 1356 in Lübeck, with the final one taking place in 1669.

text: Luoyang, 190 CE: Burned by Dong Zhuo.
evidence: In 190 ce Dong Zhuo burned Luoyang, the capital, and removed himself and the emperor to the ancient capital of Chang'an.

text: Luoyang, 25 CE: Eastern Han capital.
evidence: Liu Xiu declared himself emperor in 25, and later that year, when he captured Luoyang to be his capital, he moved to the city.

text: Luoyang, 311 CE: Sacked by Xiongnu forces.
evidence: Xiongnu soldiers led by Liu Cong conquered and pillaged the Jin capital at Luoyang and captured Emperor Huai.

text: Luoyang, 493 CE: Northern Wei move their capital here.
evidence: The Northern Wei infobox dates the move to Luoyang to 25 October 493. Other sources, including the Northern Wei article text, give 494.
fix: Sources split between 493 (the decision) and 494 (the actual move). Say 'moved 493–494' or use 494 for the move itself.

text: Luoyang, 770 BCE: Eastern Zhou move their capital here.
evidence: The sources agree that King Ping moved the Zhou capital to Luoyang around 770 BCE

text: Machu Picchu, 1911 CE: Hiram Bingham publicises it.
evidence: Bingham reached Machu Picchu in 1911, but he didn't publicize it until 1913. The entire April 1913 issue of National Geographic was devoted to it.
fix: Say that Bingham reached Machu Picchu in 1911, or date the publicising to 1913 (April 1913 National Geographic).

text: Madrid, 1561 CE: Philip II makes it capital.
evidence: Philip II moved the royal court to Madrid in 1561, making it the capital of the Spanish Empire due to its central geographic location
fix: Optional: say the capital status was de facto. The court briefly moved to Valladolid in 1601–1606.

text: Madrid, 1936 CE: Besieged in the Civil War.
evidence: Madrid was besieged from October 1936 and fell to the Nationalist armies on 28 March 1939.

text: Malacca, 1511 CE: Taken by Portugal.
evidence: Captured: 15 August 1511 (Wikipedia infobox; other sources give 24 August 1511)

text: Malacca, 1641 CE: Taken by the Dutch.
evidence: The siege began on 3 August 1640 and ended with a Portuguese surrender on 14 January 1641.

text: Manila, 1571 CE: Spanish capital founded.
evidence: Manila was capital of the Spanish East Indies from 1571 to 1898; Legazpi founded the Spanish city on 24 June 1571.

text: Manila, 1762 CE: Taken by the British.
evidence: Britain won the battle, which was followed by an eighteen-month occupation of Manila (captured 6 October 1762).

text: Manila, 1945 CE: Destroyed in the Battle of Manila.
evidence: Wikipedia calls it one of the most devastated capitals of the Second World War, alongside Berlin and Warsaw, and notes the fighting destroyed much of the city's architectural and cultural heritage.

text: Mari, 1933 CE: Excavations begin.
evidence: Excavation of the Tell Hariri, in the middle valley of the Syrian Euphrates, began in 1933.

text: Mari, 1759 BCE: Destroyed by Hammurabi.
evidence: The invasion destroyed the kingdom around 1761 BC. (The World History timeline puts the destruction between 1760 and 1757 BCE.)
fix: Optionally change 1759 to about 1761 BCE; 1759 falls inside the 1760–1757 range some sources give.

text: Marrakesh, 1147 CE: Taken by the Almohads.
evidence: The Almohad Conquest of Marrakesh occurred in 1147 when the Almohad movement seized control of the Almoravid capital.

text: Marseille, 1720 CE: Great Plague kills about half the city.
evidence: The disease killed over 100,000 people: 50,000 in the city during the next two years, plus about 50,000 in surrounding provinces and towns (from a population of 90,000).
fix: Estimates for the city range from about 39,000 to 50,000 deaths out of 90,000, so 'about half' is at the upper end. 'Roughly 40–50%' would be safer.

text: Marseille, 1869 CE: Suez Canal opens; the port booms.
evidence: 1869. Ouverture du Canal de Suez qui est un élément majeur de la richesse de la Provence et de la richesse de son activité maritime, à commencer par Marseille.

text: Marseille, 49 BCE: Besieged and taken by Caesar.
evidence: The siege ran from 19 April to 6 September 49 BC, ending in a Caesarian victory and the Roman annexation of the city.

text: Mecca, 1979 CE: Grand Mosque seizure.
evidence: The Grand Mosque seizure ran from 20 November to 4 December 1979 in Mecca.

text: Mecca, 570 CE: Birth of Muhammad (by tradition).
evidence: Muhammad was born in approximately 570 CE in Mecca.

text: Mecca, 630 CE: Taken by Muhammad's followers.
evidence: The conquest is dated to December 629 to January 630 (Ramadan 8 AH).

text: Medina, 622 CE: The Hijra: Muhammad moves here.
evidence: The term hijra designates the migration of Prophet Muhammad and his early Muslim community from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

text: Memphis, 641 CE: Arab conquest; Fustat founded nearby.
evidence: Fustat was founded in 641 by the Arab general 'Amr ibn al-'As, built next to what is now Old Cairo immediately after the Muslim conquest of Egypt.

text: Memphis, 2560 BCE: Great Pyramid built nearby.
evidence: The generally accepted estimated date of its completion is c. 2560 BC.

text: Memphis, 3100 BCE: Founded by Menes (by tradition).
evidence: The city is said to have been founded by the legendary first king of Egypt Menes in 3100 BC.

text: Memphis, 331 BCE: Alexander crowned pharaoh here.
evidence: Alexander was crowned Pharaoh at Memphis after entering Egypt in late October 332 BC. (Whether he received an elaborate coronation ceremony is debated.)
fix: Change the year to 332 BCE. He returned to Memphis in spring 331 BCE, but the coronation is dated to 332 BCE. Also, whether a formal coronation took place is disputed, since Arrian and Curtius don't mention one.

sources.cite: How Alexander the Great Became Pharaoh of Egypt | History Hit (historyhit.com)

text: Meroë, 300 BCE: Capital of Kush moves here from Napata.
evidence: King Aspelta moved the capital to Meroë, considerably farther south than Napata, possibly c. 591 BC, just after the sack of Napata by Egyptian Pharaoh Psamtik II.
fix: Change 300 BCE to about 591 BCE. The Met dates a later step to about 250 BCE, when the royal necropolis moved to Meroë, but that is not 300 BCE either.
note: Left for the owner: when the capital moved from Napata to Meroe is debated (about 591 BCE after the Egyptian sack, or the 3rd century BCE when royal burials moved).

text: Merv, 1037 CE: Taken by the Seljuks.
evidence: In 1037 the Ghaznavids were forced to cede Sarakhs, Abivard, and Merv to the Seljuks.

text: Merv, 1221 CE: Destroyed by the Mongols.
evidence: Dated to April 1221 as a Mongol victory, with the city's population massacred.

text: Merv, 651 CE: Last Sasanian king killed nearby.
evidence: He was eventually killed by a miller near Merv in 651, possibly at the instigation of the local margrave.

text: Mexico City, 1325 CE: Tenochtitlan founded.
evidence: The exact date of the founding of the city is unclear, but the date 13 March 1325 was chosen in 1925 to celebrate the 600th anniversary.

text: Mexico City, 1487 CE: Templo Mayor rededicated.
evidence: One of the most infamous is the four-day butchering of captives when Ahuitzotl re-dedicated the temple and extended it even higher in order to celebrate his imperial triumphs in 1487 CE.

text: Mexico City, 1519 CE: Cortés arrives.
evidence: The Spaniards and their Tlaxcaltec allies entered Tenochtitlan without resistance on November 8, 1519.

text: Mexico City, 1521 CE: Falls after a siege.
evidence: On 13 August 1521, the Spanish conquered Tenochtitlan, taking the new Aztec emperor Cuauhtemoc captive.

text: Mexico City, 1629 CE: Great flood lasts five years.
evidence: Parts of the city remained flooded for four years.
fix: Change to a flood that began in 1629 and left parts of the city under water for about four years. The five-year figure comes only from a newspaper column, and the Wikipedia article says four.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Rodrigo Pacheco, 3rd Marquess of Cerralvo

text: Mexico City, 1821 CE: Capital of independent Mexico.
evidence: Iturbide's army marched into the capital on September 27, and Mexico was declared independent the following day.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Army of the Three Guarantees

text: Mexico City, 1985 CE: Earthquake kills thousands.
evidence: The quake caused the deaths of at least 5,000 people (infobox range 5,000 to 45,000).

text: Milan, 1162 CE: Razed by Barbarossa.
evidence: March 6 German forces led by Frederick Barbarossa, Holy Roman Emperor, capture Milan; much of the city is destroyed three weeks later on the emperor's orders.

text: Milan, 286 CE: Western Roman capital.
evidence: Diocletian moved the Western capital from Rome to Mediolanum in 286, leaving his colleague Maximian there.

text: Milan, 313 CE: Edict of Milan.
evidence: The edict was the outcome of a political agreement concluded in Mediolanum (modern Milan) in February 313.

text: Miletus, 334 BCE: Taken by Alexander.
evidence: The siege of Miletus was Alexander the Great's first siege and naval encounter with the Achaemenid Empire.

text: Miletus, 494 BCE: Sacked by the Persians.
evidence: Eventually the city was captured, and devastated.

text: Miletus, 585 BCE: Thales predicts a solar eclipse (by tradition).
evidence: Herodotus reports that this change from daylight to darkness had been foretold to the Ionians by Thales of Miletus, who fixed the date for it within the limits of the year.

text: Mohenjo-daro, 1922 CE: Excavations begin.
evidence: Banerji excavated Mohenjo-Daro in December 1922, and he continued excavating this site up to January, February and March 1923.

sources.cite: glimpses of the first excavation of mohenjodaro in 1922 (thefridaytimes.com)

text: Mohenjo-daro, 2500 BCE: Great Bath built.
evidence: The bath was constructed in the third millennium BCE, shortly after the citadel mound it sits on was raised.
fix: Optionally write 'c. 2500 BCE (3rd millennium)'. Britannica gives 3000 BCE, so the exact date is loose.

text: Mombasa, 1593 CE: Portuguese build Fort Jesus.
evidence: The Fort, built by the Portuguese in 1593-1596 to the designs of Giovanni Battista Cairati to protect the port of Mombasa.

sources.cite: Fort Jesus, Mombasa (UNESCO World Heritage Centre) (whc.unesco.org)

text: Mombasa, 1698 CE: Taken by Oman.
evidence: The Omani siege of Mombasa ran from 13 March 1696 to 13 December 1698, led by Saif I bin Sultan, and the fort fell to the Omanis in December 1698.

text: Moscow, 1238 CE: Burned by the Mongols.
evidence: The siege ran 15–20 January 1238 and ended in a Mongol victory; the village was taken after 5 days of siege.

text: Moscow, 1480 CE: Ends Mongol overlordship.
evidence: The standoff ran from 8 October to 11 November 1480 and traditionally marks the end of Mongol rule over Russia.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Great Stand on the Ugra River

text: Moscow, 1571 CE: Burned by Crimean Tatars.
evidence: The Fire of Moscow occurred on 24 May 1571 during the Crimean raid led by Devlet I Giray.

text: Moscow, 1812 CE: Burns as Napoleon arrives.
evidence: Napoleon's army entered Moscow on September 14, 1812; fires broke out that night, apparently set by Russian patriots.

text: Moscow, 1918 CE: Capital again under the Bolsheviks.
evidence: in 1918 the Soviet government moved the capital to Moscow

sources.cite: MIA: Encyclopedia of Marxism: Glossary of Places (marxists.org)

text: Mumbai, 1661 CE: Given to England as a royal dowry.
evidence: The Seven Islands of Bombay were partly handed over to England under this title as part of the dowry of Catherine Braganza.

text: Mumbai, 1853 CE: Asia's first passenger railway.
evidence: The original 21 miles (33.8 km) section opened in 1853, between Bombay (Mumbai) and Tanna (now Thane)
fix: Say 'India's first passenger railway (16 April 1853, Bombay to Thane)'. Only one weaker source calls it Asia's first.

text: Mumbai, 1896 CE: Plague outbreak.
evidence: Bombay's municipal administration announced plague in the city in September 1896

text: Mycenae, 1876 CE: Schliemann finds the shaft graves.
evidence: It held six shaft graves, and five of which were excavated by H. Schliemann in 1876 and one by P. Stamatakis in the following year.

text: Mycenae, 1200 BCE: Palace burned.
evidence: the palace itself was destroyed around 1180 BC, possibly by fire
fix: Change the date to about 1180 BCE and say 'possibly by fire'. The palaces generally declined around 1200 BCE.

text: Mycenae, 1250 BCE: Lion Gate built.
evidence: It was erected during the thirteenth century BC, around 1250 BC, in the northwestern side of the acropolis.

text: Nanjing, 1368 CE: Ming capital.
evidence: Zhu proclaimed the Ming dynasty; with himself as the first emperor, known as the Hongwu Emperor; and that Jiankang, now Yingtian, was the "southern capital".

text: Nanjing, 1421 CE: Ming court moves to Beijing.
evidence: On 28 October 1420, Beijing was officially declared the principal capital of the empire, and by February 1421, ministries and other government agencies had relocated to Beijing.

text: Nanjing, 1853 CE: Taiping capital.
evidence: On 19 March 1853, the Taiping Army seized Nanjing, renamed it Tianjing, and made it their new capital.

text: Nanjing, 1937 CE: Nanjing Massacre.
evidence: Mass rape and murder, between December 1937 and March 1938, of Chinese civilians, noncombatants, and prisoners of war by the Imperial Japanese Army in Nanjing, then the capital of the Republic of China.

text: Nanjing, 589 CE: Razed by the Sui.
evidence: The city was razed to the ground, while Sui troops escorted Chen nobles back north.

text: Naples, 1224 CE: University founded.
evidence: Frederick II of Hohenstaufen, King of Sicily and Holy Roman Emperor established the University of Naples as the Studium with an Imperial Charter, on 5 June 1224.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, University of Naples Federico II

text: Naples, 1656 CE: Plague kills about half.
evidence: Around 150,000–200,000 people died in 1656, which accounted for at least half of the local population.
fix: Optional: note that some sources put the toll nearer a third (about 100,000).

text: Naples, 1860 CE: Joins united Italy.
evidence: Garibaldi ... entered Naples on September 7th; the kingdom was annexed by plebiscite, completing the first phase of Italian unification.
fix: The quote is a paraphrase of the search summary, not the page's wording. Annexation followed the 1860 plebiscite, and the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Kingdom of the Two Sicilies

text: Nara-shi, 752 CE: Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji dedicated.
evidence: On May 26, 752, Japan's political, military, and monastic forces gathered to witness the eye-opening ceremony.
fix: The year 752 is supported. Sources differ on the day: this page says 26 May and another says 9 April.

sources.cite: The World on Stage: Multicultural Music and Dance at Tōdai-ji Temple's Eye-Opening Ceremony (soas.ac.uk)

text: Nara-shi, 784 CE: Court leaves.
evidence: Emperor Kanmu established a new capital Nagaoka-kyō at Nagaoka in 784, before moving to Heian-kyō, Kyoto, a decade later in 794.

text: New York City, 1626 CE: Dutch 'buy' Manhattan.
evidence: The scholarly consensus is that the purchase did take place, probably by Peter Minuit, and most likely in mid-May, 1626.

text: New York City, 1664 CE: Taken by England, renamed New York.
evidence: Manhattan was taken on September 8th, 1664, and the city was renamed for the Duke of York.

text: New York City, 1825 CE: Erie Canal opens.
evidence: The canal was completed on Oct. 26, 1825 after eight years of construction.

text: New York City, 1898 CE: Five boroughs merge.
evidence: The consolidation took effect on January 1, 1898, when Manhattan, Brooklyn, the Bronx, Queens, and Staten Island were combined into one city.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Boroughs of New York City

text: New York City, 2001 CE: September 11 attacks.
evidence: Two of the airliners were flown into the World Trade Centre in New York City, one into each tower.

text: Nineveh, 612 BCE: Sacked by Medes and Babylonians.
evidence: In 612 BC, their combined armies attacked and razed Nineveh, the Assyrian capital.

text: Nineveh, 650 BCE: Ashurbanipal gathers his library.
evidence: Guinness World Records gives the library's assembly as between 668 and 631 BCE.
fix: The founding date is uncertain. One scholarly account says the library was probably built up toward the end of his reign, after the 647 BCE Elam campaign. 650 BCE falls inside the collecting period, so a range such as 668–631 BCE would be safer.

text: Nineveh, 700 BCE: Sennacherib makes it his capital.
evidence: Nineveh (705–612 BCE)

text: Nishapur, 1221 CE: Mongols kill most of its people.
evidence: after the city's surrender, the entire population was driven out on the plain and put to the sword, excluding a small number of artisans and children.

text: Novgorod, 1136 CE: Becomes a merchant republic.
evidence: the city revolted against his rule and achieved its political independence as a feudal republic in 1136.

text: Novgorod, 1478 CE: Annexed by Moscow.
evidence: Novgorod's independence ended in 1478, when Ivan III's forces besieged the city and it surrendered.

text: Novgorod, 1570 CE: Massacred by Ivan the Terrible.
evidence: The massacre of Novgorod took place from 2 January to 12 February 1570.

text: Osaka, 1583 CE: Hideyoshi builds Osaka Castle.
evidence: The construction of Osaka Castle started in 1583 on the former site of the Ishiyama Honganji Temple.

text: Osaka, 1615 CE: Siege of Osaka.
evidence: On June 5, 1615, Tokugawa attacked Osaka Castle. The castle fell, and Hideyori and his mother committed seppuku.
fix: The siege ran in two stages, winter 1614 and summer 1615. 1615 is the year it ended.

text: Osaka, 1730 CE: Dōjima rice futures market licensed.
evidence: officially approved as "Dojima Rice Exchange" by Japan's shogunate government in 1730

text: Palenque, 1952 CE: Pakal's tomb found.
evidence: Pakal's tomb was found in 1952 inside the Temple of the Inscriptions at Palenque, by Mexican archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier.

text: Palenque, 615 CE: Pakal the Great takes the throne.
evidence: Wikipedia gives his coronation as 27 July 615, and his reign as ending with his death on 29 August 683.

text: Paris, 1163 CE: Notre-Dame begun.
evidence: Work began in 1163 under Bishop Maurice de Sully and was largely finished by about 1260, with later changes.

text: Paris, 1348 CE: Black Death.
evidence: A Sortiraparis article places the arrival in late summer 1348, and a Jean de Venette chronicle describes events in Paris in August 1348.

sources.cite: Ephemeris of August 28 in Paris: The Black Death epidemic (sortiraparis.com)

text: Paris, 1789 CE: Storming of the Bastille.
evidence: The Storming of the Bastille refers to revolutionary insurgents storming and seizing control of the medieval armory, fortress, and political prison known as the Bastille (14 July 1789).

text: Paris, 1853 CE: Haussmann rebuilds the city.
evidence: Haussmann was chosen by Emperor Napoleon III to carry out a massive urban renewal programme of new boulevards, parks and public works in Paris, serving as prefect of the Seine from 1853 to 1870.

text: Paris, 1871 CE: Paris Commune.
evidence: The Paris Commune was a short-lived revolutionary government that ruled Paris from 18 March to 28 May 1871.

text: Paris, 1940 CE: German occupation.
evidence: The French government departed Paris on June 10, and the Germans occupied the city on June 14 [1940].

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Paris in World War II

text: Paris, 508 CE: Clovis makes it his capital.
fix: Optional: note that some sources date it to 509.

text: Paris, 845 CE: Viking siege.
evidence: Viking forces were led by a chieftain called "Reginherus"

text: Pasargadae, 330 BCE: Alexander visits Cyrus's tomb.
evidence: Alexander found the tomb of Cyrus, son of Cambyses, broken into and robbed
fix: The search summary says Arrian places the tomb visit in early 324 BCE. 330 BCE is the year of the Persian conquest. Change the date to 324 BCE.

sources.cite: Arrian on the tomb of Cyrus (livius.org)

text: Pasargadae, 546 BCE: Cyrus begins his capital.
evidence: work on Pasargadae began around 546 BCE under Cyrus

text: Patna, 1541 CE: Sher Shah Suri rebuilds it as Patna.
evidence: built a fort there in 1541, transferred the provincial capital from Bihar Sharif, and gave it the new name of Patna

text: Patna, 320 CE: Gupta empire capital.
evidence: capital of the Gupta Empire (c. 320–550 CE)

text: Patna, 268 BCE: Ashoka rules from here.
evidence: Ashoka ruled from the same city... ca. 268–232 BCE

text: Patna, 321 BCE: Chandragupta Maurya's capital.
evidence: he established his capital in Pataliputra (present-day Patna)
fix: Sources give 322 or 321 BCE for the founding of the Mauryan empire, so 321 is within tolerance.

text: Persepolis, 330 BCE: Burned by Alexander's army.
evidence: After looting the city, Alexander's forces set fire to the palace complex and the surrounding city (330 BCE).

sources.cite: Alexander the Great & the Burning of Persepolis (worldhistory.org)

text: Persepolis, 518 BCE: Darius I begins building.
evidence: Darius I begins construction of Persepolis (approximate date); another source gives construction beginning between 518-515 BCE.

text: Petra, 106 CE: Annexed by Rome.
evidence: remained an independent political entity from the mid-3rd century BC until it was annexed in AD 106 by the Roman Empire, which renamed it to Arabia Petraea

text: Petra, 1812 CE: Burckhardt reaches it.
evidence: Johann Ludwig Burckhardt, a Swiss orientalist, reached Petra on 22 August 1812, the first European to see the city since the Crusades.

sources.cite: The man who discovered a lost wonder of the world (cam.ac.uk)

text: Petra, 363 CE: Earthquake.
evidence: Cyril of Jerusalem wrote that "more than half of Petra (RQM)" was "overthrown" in the 363 CE earthquakes.

text: Philadelphia, 1776 CE: Declaration of Independence.
evidence: Congress approved the Declaration of Independence and ordered it printed on July 4, 1776, at the Pennsylvania State House (Independence Hall) in Philadelphia.

text: Philadelphia, 1787 CE: Constitution written.
evidence: The Constitutional Convention met in Philadelphia from May 25 to September 17, 1787, at the Pennsylvania State House; the delegates wrote a new constitution.

text: Plovdiv, 1364 CE: Ottoman conquest.
evidence: The Ottoman Turks under Lala Shakhin Pasha seize Plovdiv (1364); the Filibe article gives 1363 or 1364.

text: Plovdiv, 1885 CE: Joins Bulgaria.
evidence: In 1885, Plovdiv and Eastern Rumelia joined Bulgaria.

text: Plovdiv, 250 CE: Sacked by Goths.
evidence: Battle of Philippopolis in 250/251 CE, after which the town was sacked by the Goths.

text: Plovdiv, 342 BCE: Philip II takes it, renames it Philippopolis.
evidence: Philip II conquered the city in 342 BC and renamed it Philippopolis in his own honour.

text: Pompeii, 1748 CE: Excavations begin.
evidence: The excavations officially started in 1748 under the King of Naples, Charles III of Bourbon.

text: Pompeii, 62 CE: Earthquake damages the town.
evidence: A violent earthquake struck in 62 AD; reconstruction works were still on going at the moment of the terrible eruption of Vesuvius in 79 AD.

text: Pompeii, 79 CE: Vesuvius erupts.
evidence: the terrible eruption of Vesuvius in 79 AD that buried the city under ash and lapilli

text: Potosí, 1545 CE: Silver found at Cerro Rico.
evidence: mining dates from the discovery of silver ores in the upper reaches of the Cerro Rico (Rich Hill) in 1545

text: Potosí, 1572 CE: Mercury refining boosts output.
evidence: it was only with the construction of large-scale mercury amalgamation facilities after 1572 that the silver potential of these ores was unlocked

text: Prague, 1348 CE: Charles University founded.
evidence: most Czech sources since the 19th century prefer to give 1348 as the year of the founding of the university

text: Prague, 1419 CE: First Defenestration.
evidence: The First Defenestration of Prague took place on 30 July 1419 at Prague's New Town Hall.

text: Prague, 1618 CE: Defenestration starts the Thirty Years' War.
evidence: On May 23, 1618, Bohemian Protestant nobles threw two Catholic imperial regents and a secretary out of a window at Prague Castle, and the event helped spark the Thirty Years' War.

text: Prague, 1968 CE: Prague Spring crushed.
evidence: The invasion began on the night of 20–21 August 1968.

sources.cite: On this day in 1968: Moscow crushes the Prague Spring (cityam.com)

text: Québec, 1759 CE: Falls to the British.
evidence: Quebec surrendered on 18 September, five days after the Battle of the Plains of Abraham on 13 September 1759.

sources.cite: battle of the plains of abraham (thecanadianencyclopedia.ca)

text: Ravenser Odd, 1362 CE: Grote Mandrenke storm.
evidence: The January 1362 storm mostly destroyed what remained of the town.

text: Rayy, 1220 CE: Destroyed by the Mongols.
evidence: In 1220 the city was almost entirely destroyed by the Mongols, and its inhabitants were massacred.

text: Rio de Janeiro, 1808 CE: Portuguese court arrives from Lisbon.
evidence: The court reached Rio de Janeiro in March 1808 (7, 8 or 11 March depending on the source), after first landing at Salvador on 22 January 1808.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Transfer of the Portuguese court to Brazil

text: Rio de Janeiro, 1960 CE: Capital moves to Brasília.
evidence: Brasília was founded by President Juscelino Kubitschek on 21 April 1960 to replace Rio de Janeiro as the national capital.

text: Rome, 1527 CE: Sacked by imperial troops.
evidence: Britannica says the attack was not ordered by the emperor, but launched on the initiative of imperial troops angry at not being paid.

text: Rome, 1871 CE: Capital of unified Italy.
evidence: The Italian Parliament approved the move of the capital from Florence to Rome in February 1871, and the Court, Senate and Chamber of Deputies moved to Rome in July.

sources.cite: Did you know: Rome wasn't Italy's first capital city? (thelocal.it)

text: Rome, 410 CE: Sacked by Visigoths.
evidence: The sack took place on 24 August 410, when Alaric's Visigoths entered the city.

text: Rome, 455 CE: Sacked by Vandals.
evidence: Gaiseric (Genseric) was king of the Vandals and Alans from 428 to 477. He conquered a large part of Roman Africa and in 455 sacked Rome.

text: Rome, 476 CE: Last western emperor deposed.
evidence: Romulus Augustulus was deposed on 4 September 476 by Odoacer, and he is generally regarded as the last Western Roman emperor.
fix: The deposition took place at Ravenna, not Rome. Reword the claim so it doesn't suggest it happened in the city of Rome.

text: Rome, 64 CE: Great Fire.
evidence: The Great Fire of Rome started on the evening of 18–19 July AD 64.

text: Rome, 800 CE: Charlemagne crowned emperor here.
evidence: At Mass, on Christmas Day (December 25), when Charlemagne knelt at the altar to pray, the pope crowned him Imperator Romanorum ("Emperor of the Romans") in Saint Peter's Basilica.

text: Rome, 27 BCE: Augustus becomes first emperor.
evidence: He reigned as the first Roman emperor from 27 BC until his death in AD 14.

text: Rome, 390 BCE: Sacked by Gauls.
evidence: Wikipedia gives 390 BC as the traditional date for the battle and sack, but notes that 387 BC is the probable date.
fix: Optionally label 390 BCE as the traditional date, since 387 BCE is probably the real one.

text: Rome, 509 BCE: Republic founded (by tradition).
evidence: Britannica describes the Republic as beginning in 509 BCE, when the Romans replaced their monarchy with elected magistrates.

text: Salvador, 1763 CE: Capital of Brazil moves to Rio.
evidence: The State of Brazil became a Viceroyalty in January 1763, when its capital was transferred from Salvador to Rio de Janeiro.

text: Samarkand, 1220 CE: Destroyed by Genghis Khan.
evidence: The siege began in March 1220 during the Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire.
fix: Optionally say 'sacked' or 'devastated'. The city was rebuilt later, and sources describe heavy destruction rather than total erasure.

text: Samarkand, 1370 CE: Timur makes it his capital.
evidence: 1370 is listed as the year the city became capital of the Timurid Empire, and Timur had made it his residence the year before.

text: Samarkand, 1417 CE: Ulugh Beg's madrasa begun.
evidence: It was built between 1417 and 1421.

text: Samarkand, 1868 CE: Taken by Russia.
evidence: The Russian army commanded by Konstantin Kaufmann took Samarkand on May 2, 1868, after a brief battle on the heights of Chupan-Ata.

text: Samarkand, 751 CE: Paper-making arrives after the Battle of Talas.
evidence: The Samarkand paper article calls the origin likely apocryphal, given significant archaeological findings of paper in the region that predate the battle.
fix: Say that Samarkand papermaking is traditionally tied to Chinese prisoners taken at Talas in 751. Add that this is disputed, because paper was already known in the region before the battle.

text: Samarkand, 329 BCE: Taken by Alexander.
evidence: A Wikipedia timeline lists the city as sacked by Alexander in 329 BCE.

text: Sanaa, 2014 CE: Taken by the Houthis.
evidence: Wikipedia lists a Houthi victory, the fall of Sanaa, and the resignation of Prime Minister Basindawa (September 2014).

text: Sarai, 1333 CE: Ibn Battuta visits.
evidence: Most sources point to 1333 for Ibn Battuta's visit to Sarai, though one dates it to 1334.

text: Sarai, 1395 CE: Destroyed by Timur.
evidence: Timur invaded the Horde's territory in 1395, destroyed Sarai Berke, and deported most of the region's skilled craftsmen to Central Asia.

text: Sardis, 1402 CE: Destroyed by Timur's army.
evidence: The city was obliterated in 1402 by the Turkic conqueror Timur (Tamerlane).

text: Sardis, 546 BCE: Croesus defeated by Cyrus.
evidence: 546 BC — Croesus, Lydian king, is defeated by Cyrus of Persia near the River Halys.

text: Seoul, 1592 CE: Burned in the Japanese invasion.
evidence: During the seven-year invasions, palaces, shrines, most government offices, licensed stores and private homes were plundered or burnt to ashes.

sources.cite: Establishment of the King's Residence (Seoul Museum of History) (museum.seoul.go.kr)

text: Seoul, 1910 CE: Japanese annexation.
evidence: The treaty was sealed on August 22, 1910, and took effect on August 29, 1910.

text: Seoul, 1950 CE: Changes hands four times in the Korean War.
evidence: Elements of the South Korean 1st Infantry Division and the US 3rd Infantry Division liberated Seoul during the night of March 14–15, marking the fourth and last time the capital would have changed hands since June 1950.
fix: The four changes of hands run from June 1950 to March 1951, so the claim could say 1950–51.

text: Seville, 1248 CE: Taken by Castile.
evidence: The siege of Seville (July 1247 – November 1248) was a 16-month successful investment during the Reconquista of Seville by forces of Ferdinand III of Castile.

text: Seville, 1503 CE: Casa de Contratación: monopoly on the Americas trade.
evidence: Its supremacy was officially established in 1503, when a royal decree awarded Seville's Puerto de Indias a trade monopoly on all goods imported from the Americas.

text: Seville, 1649 CE: Plague kills almost half.
evidence: a catastrophic plague in 1649 reduced that population by almost half
fix: Estimates vary. Wikipedia's Great Plague of Seville gives about 150,000 dead of 600,000 across the city and its rural districts, roughly a quarter. A Universidad de Málaga journal article and a Fundació Uriach entry give about 60,000 dead, or 46%, for the city. The claim could say 'about half of the city'.

text: Singapore, 1819 CE: Raffles founds a British trading post.
evidence: Sources describe Raffles establishing a British trading post in 1819.

text: Singapore, 1942 CE: Falls to Japan.
evidence: The Japanese captured the island in February 1942 (fall of Singapore on 15 February 1942).

text: Singapore, 1965 CE: Independence.
evidence: Singapore became an independent republic on 9 August 1965.

text: Saint Petersburg, 1712 CE: Capital of Russia.
fix: Optional: say the capital moved back to Moscow in 1728 and returned to Saint Petersburg in 1732. It stayed the capital until 1918.

text: Saint Petersburg, 1905 CE: Bloody Sunday.
evidence: Bloody Sunday (22 January 1905, Old Style 9 January) was a massacre in St. Petersburg in which imperial troops fired on unarmed demonstrators marching toward the Winter Palace.

text: Saint Petersburg, 1917 CE: Revolutions.
evidence: It took place through an armed insurrection in Petrograd on 7 November 1917 [O.S. 25 October].

text: Saint Petersburg, 1918 CE: Capital moves to Moscow.
evidence: Moscow once again became the capital, now of the Soviet state, on 12 March 1918.

sources.cite: Moscow becomes the capital of the Soviet state (prlib.ru)

text: Saint Petersburg, 1941 CE: Siege of Leningrad begins.
evidence: Date: 8 September 1941 – 27 January 1944

text: Sybaris, 510 BCE: Destroyed by Croton.
evidence: about 510 B.C. by Croton, her next door neighbor and rival to the south

text: Syracuse, Sicily, 878 CE: Sacked by the Aghlabids.
evidence: The city, effectively left without assistance by the central Byzantine government, was taken by the Aghlabid forces.
fix: The siege began in August 877 and the city fell on 21 May 878.

text: Syracuse, Sicily, 212 BCE: Taken by Rome; Archimedes killed.
evidence: A Roman soldier who broke into his home during the sack killed him.
fix: Optional: some sources date the fall to autumn 212 or spring 211 BCE.

text: Syracuse, Sicily, 413 BCE: Destroys the Athenian expedition.
evidence: Athens sent a massive expeditionary force to attack Syracuse, but it was eventually annihilated.

text: Tehran, 1786 CE: Qajar capital.
evidence: Agha Mohammad Khan made Tehran Iran's capital in 1786, and it has stayed the capital since.

text: Tehran, 1979 CE: Iranian Revolution.
evidence: By 11 February 1979 the monarchy had collapsed, and the result was the establishment of the Islamic Republic of Iran.

text: Teotihuacan, 378 CE: Its envoys take over Tikal.
evidence: Sihyaj K'ahk' arrived at Tikal in January 378 CE, the day Chak Tok Ich'aak died, as the representative of Teotihuacan's power in Petén.
fix: The arrival is well attested, but scholars debate whether it was a conquest or a political installation. Consider wording such as 'Teotihuacan-backed envoy arrives at Tikal'.

sources.cite: Naachtun's Stela 24 and the Entrada of 378 (mayadecipherment.com)

text: Teotihuacan, 550 CE: City centre burned.
evidence: The population of Teotihuacan dropped 70-80% when the center of the city and all the temples were burned in what's referred to as the 'Great Fire Event.'

sources.cite: Search for clues may explain the collapse of ancient city in Mexico (newswise.com)

text: Thessaloniki, 1430 CE: Ottoman conquest.
evidence: The siege began on 29 March 1430 and lasted three days, and about 7,000 inhabitants were enslaved.

text: Thessaloniki, 1917 CE: Great Fire.
evidence: The fire began on 18 August 1917 and burned for 32 hours, leaving more than 70,000 people homeless.

text: Thessaloniki, 1943 CE: Its Jewish community deported.
evidence: Between 15 March and 10 August 1943, over forty thousand members of the Jewish community of Thessaloniki were rounded up by occupying German forces and deported to the death camp of Auschwitz-Birkenau.

sources.cite: Thessaloniki Jews to mark 70th anniversary of Nazi deportations (jta.org)

text: Thessaloniki, 390 CE: Massacre ordered by Theodosius.
evidence: The Massacre of Thessalonica is believed to have taken place around 390

text: Tikal, 378 CE: Teotihuacan-backed takeover.
evidence: the dynasty's trajectory changed significantly with Chak Tok Ich'aak I's death in 378 CE, leading to the installation of rulers from Teotihuacán
fix: Optionally say "Teotihuacan-linked takeover". Scholars debate whether it was conquest or something else.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, List of lords of Tikal

text: Tikal, 562 CE: Defeated by Caracol.
evidence: An altar at Caracol records Tikal's defeat in A.D. 562.

text: Tikal, 695 CE: Defeats rival Calakmul.
evidence: In 695 Calakmul suffered a military defeat at the hands of Tikal

text: Tikal, 869 CE: Last dated monument.
evidence: Stela 11 carries the Long Count date 10.2.0.0.0, which correlates to August 15, 869

text: Timbuktu, 1325 CE: Mansa Musa's Djinguereber Mosque.
evidence: Heinrich Barth reported an inscription above the main door said to show the date 1327 and Mansa Musa's name.
fix: Change the year to 1327, when the mosque was completed. Mansa Musa returned from Mecca in 1325, and the mosque was built after that. The architect al-Sahili's role is disputed.

text: Timbuktu, 1591 CE: Moroccan invasion.
evidence: The Battle of Tondibi was in March 1591. Judar Pasha reached Timbuktu in April 1591.

text: Tokyo, 1603 CE: Seat of the Tokugawa shogunate.
evidence: Ieyasu formally founded the Tokugawa shogunate in 1603 and established his headquarters at Edo Castle.
fix: The city was called Edo until 1868, so write "Edo (later Tokyo)".

text: Tokyo, 1657 CE: Meireki fire.
evidence: The fire struck Edo (now Tokyo) on 2 March 1657, in the third year of the Meireki era.

text: Tokyo, 1868 CE: Renamed Tokyo; the emperor arrives.
evidence: Emperor Meiji announces that the name of the city of Edo was being changed to Tokyo, or "eastern capital".

text: Tokyo, 1923 CE: Great Kantō earthquake.
evidence: The Great Kantō earthquake struck the Kantō Plain on Honshu on 1 September 1923, with a magnitude of about 8.0 and its epicenter roughly 100 km southwest of Tokyo.

text: Tokyo, 1945 CE: Firebombing.
evidence: The March 1945 firebombing of Tokyo, codenamed Operation Meetinghouse, was a U.S. raid on the night of March 9-10.

text: Trier, 306 CE: Constantine rules from here.
evidence: The city of Augusta Treverorum (Trier) served as his principal residence for the next six years.

text: Troy, 1871 CE: Schliemann starts digging.
evidence: In October–November 1871, Heinrich Schliemann "officially" began excavating the site by digging into the northern side of Hisarlik.

text: Troy, 1180 BCE: Troy VIIa destroyed.
evidence: Jordan's page gives 1180 (or 1183) for the destruction of Troy VIIa.

text: Troy, 334 BCE: Alexander visits.
evidence: Alexander's 334 BC visit to Troy is well documented; he sacrificed to Athena and honored Achilles' tomb at the start of his campaign against Persia.

sources.cite: Plutarch on Alexander's visit to Troy (livius.org)

text: Tunis, 1535 CE: Taken by Charles V.
evidence: Charles personally led the great invasion fleet and 25,000-man army that sailed from Barcelona to take Tunis in 1535

text: Tunis, 1881 CE: French protectorate.
evidence: The Treaty of Bardo, signed on 12 May 1881, set up the French protectorate over Tunisia.

text: Tyre, Lebanon, 1291 CE: Taken by the Mamluks.
evidence: After a long siege, the city was captured by the Mamluks in 1291.

text: Tyre, Lebanon, 332 BCE: Alexander's seven-month siege.
evidence: The Macedonians first blockaded and besieged Tyre for seven months before building a causeway to reach the island city.

text: Ugarit, 1928 CE: A farmer's plough uncovers a tomb.
evidence: A farmer plowing a field struck a hard object... overturning it revealed a passage to a tomb... in the spring of 1928.

sources.cite: The Archives Of Ugarit -- By: G. Herbert Livingston (galaxie.com)

text: Ugarit, 1185 BCE: Destroyed in the Bronze Age collapse.
evidence: Wikipedia lists the city as abandoned around 1185 BC, along with the sites of many other polities that fell in the Late Bronze Age collapse.
fix: Optional: note that archaeological and radiocarbon work puts the destruction slightly earlier, about 1192–1190 BCE.

text: Ur, 2004 BCE: Sacked by the Elamites.
evidence: Ur's fall is dated to 2004 BC in the Middle chronology, or 1940 BC in the Short chronology.
fix: Optional: say 'Middle chronology' because the Short chronology dates the fall to about 1940 BCE.

text: Ur, 2100 BCE: Ur-Nammu builds the Great Ziggurat.
evidence: The Ziggurat was part of larger temple complex, built in 2100 BCE by King Ur-Nammu who dedicated in honour of Nanna/Sîn and rebuilt in 600 BC by Nabonidus.

text: Ur, 2600 BCE: Royal Tombs, with their gold and lyres.
evidence: These lyres were found in queen Pu-Abi's grave, inside the "Great Death-Pit", one of the graves in the Royal Cemetery at Ur. Early dynastic period, 2600-2400 BCE.

sources.cite: The Silver and Golden Lyres from Ur (worldhistory.org)

text: Uruk, 2700 BCE: Gilgamesh may have ruled here.
evidence: His rule probably would have taken place sometime in the beginning of the Early Dynastic Period

text: Uruk, 3200 BCE: Earliest proto-cuneiform tablets.
evidence: This system is documented by around 5,000 clay tablets coming from various sites, dating from c. 3350–3000BC.

text: Varanasi, 1194 CE: Ghurid armies sack its temples.
evidence: The original temple was allegedly uprooted by Ghurids in 1193/1194 CE, and the Razia Mosque was constructed in its place.
fix: Optional: note that the scale of the destruction comes from later chronicles and is debated.

text: Varanasi, 1669 CE: Aurangzeb destroys the Vishwanath temple.
evidence: Several historical accounts place the demolition order in 1669.

text: Varanasi, 1780 CE: Kashi Vishwanath temple rebuilt.
evidence: The present structure was put up on an adjacent site in 1780 by the Maratha ruler Ahilyabai Holkar.
fix: Optional: say it was built on an adjacent site, next to the Gyanvapi Mosque.

text: Varanasi, 528 BCE: The Buddha's first sermon at Sarnath (by tradition).
fix: The sources I found only say 6th or 5th century BCE, and I found no page giving 528 BCE. Change the date to 'c. 6th–5th century BCE' or cite a source for 528.

sources.cite: The Buddha's First Sermon in Sarnath (getty.edu)

text: Venice, 1204 CE: Leads the sack of Constantinople.
evidence: Crusaders took Constantinople between 12 and 15 April 1204; the Venetian doge Enrico Dandolo had a decisive role in the Fourth Crusade and the sack.
fix: Optional: say Venice helped lead the Fourth Crusade's sack, since the army was a joint crusader-Venetian force.

text: Venice, 1348 CE: Black Death.
evidence: When the plague reached Venice in January 1348, the city council appointed a crisis committee to deal with the situation.

text: Venice, 1498 CE: Da Gama reaches India, undercutting its spice trade.
evidence: The opening of a new route to India, land of spices, appears of the greatest importance to Venice since venetian prosperity depended on levantine spice trade.
fix: Optional: say da Gama reached Calicut in May 1498. Scholars debate how lasting the damage to the Levant spice trade was.

text: Venice, 1575 CE: Plague kills about a third.
evidence: The most common estimate is about 50,000 deaths, roughly a third of the population (this is the search summary's wording, not a verbatim page sentence).
fix: Optional: the epidemic ran 1575–1577. Lapham's Quarterly gives a range of a quarter to a third.

text: Venice, 1797 CE: Napoleon ends the Republic.
evidence: Ludovico Manin was the 120th and last Doge of Venice... until its fall on 12 May 1797, when he was forced to abdicate by Napoleon Bonaparte.

text: Venice, 697 CE: First doge (by tradition).
evidence: Anafesto was, according to John the Deacon and other later traditions, the first Doge of Venice, serving (allegedly) from 697 to 717.

text: Vienna, 1529 CE: Ottoman siege fails.
evidence: On October 15, Suleiman then ordered a retreat of his battered army, which turned into a disastrous ordeal as winter snows came early, causing many deaths.

text: Vienna, 1683 CE: Second Ottoman siege broken.
evidence: The siege ran from 14 July – 11 September 1683, and the decisive battle took place on 12 September, when a Christian coalition led by Polish king John III Sobieski won (this is the search summary's wording).

text: Vienna, 1815 CE: Congress of Vienna.
evidence: The Final Act was signed nine days before Waterloo, on June 18, 1815 (New World Encyclopedia; this is the search summary's wording). Britannica's student article says the congress opened in September 1814 and ended in June 1815.
fix: Optional: say 1814–15, with the Final Act signed in June 1815.

text: Vienna, 1918 CE: Habsburg empire collapses.
evidence: Karl renounced all part in conducting the business of the State on 11 November 1918.

text: Vijayanagara (Hampi), 1509 CE: Krishnadevaraya's golden age begins.
evidence: Wikipedia gives his reign as 26 July 1509 – 17 October 1529.

text: Vijayanagara (Hampi), 1565 CE: Battle of Talikota; city sacked.
evidence: The Sultanates' armies went on to plunder Vijayanagara, unopposed.

text: Warsaw, 1596 CE: Becomes capital.
evidence: Warsaw became the capital of the Commonwealth and of the Polish Crown in 1596, when King Sigismund III Vasa moved the court from Kraków.
fix: Optional: Britannica and the same Wikipedia article say the king moved there for good in 1611, so 1596 is the official move and 1611 is the final settling.

text: Warsaw, 1944 CE: Uprising crushed; city razed.
evidence: On 2 October 1944, delegates of the Home Army (AK) Headquarters signed the act of surrender; Himmler ordered that Warsaw be razed to the ground.

text: Xi’an, 1974 CE: Terracotta Army found.
evidence: Britannica says the tomb chamber was found in March 1974, when farmers drilling a well discovered a subterranean chamber near Xi'an.

text: Xi’an, 618 CE: Tang capital.
evidence: In 618 the Tang moved into the same walls and restored the name Chang'an.

sources.cite: Chang'an (Silk Road Seattle, University of Washington) (depts.washington.edu)

text: Xi’an, 756 CE: An Lushan's rebels take the city.
evidence: He then captured Chang'an, the western capital, in July 756.

Abydos (Egypt) was a city from about ? to today.

text: Akhetaten (Amarna) (Egypt) was a city from about 1346 BCE to about 1332 BCE. Brand-new capital built by Akhenaten for the sun-disc god Aten. Abandoned within about 15 years, soon after Akhenaten died and the old gods returned.

Aksum (Ethiopia) was a city from about 100 BCE to today. Capital of the Aksumite kingdom, famous for its giant carved stelae. King Ezana's conversion around 330 made it one of the first Christian states.
evidence: The emperor Ezana converted to Christianity around 330 A.D., making Aksum into one of the earliest Christian states.
fix: The Ezana conversion around 330 and the stelae are supported. No page I found gives a founding date, so the 100 BCE start is unconfirmed.

sources.cite: monumental architecture and stelae of the aksumite empire (metmuseum.org)

text: Yin (Anyang) (China) was a city from about 1300 BCE to about 1046 BCE. Last capital of the Shang dynasty. Its oracle bones carry China's earliest writing; the Zhou conquest ended it.
